seo.title: Architecture — OpenMixer
seo.description: A technical overview of OpenMixer: one canonical model, one REST door with live streams, one native PipeWire node carrying the audio, and a C signal-processing core.

hero.title: One model. One door. One path to audio.
hero.lede: This page explains how OpenMixer is put together and why it is put together that way. It is written for someone deciding whether to build on it, run it, or take it apart.

s1.title: The server owns console state. Clients render it.
s1.p1: There is one canonical mixer model — channels, faders, buses, sends, DCAs, the matrix, latency paths, sessions — and it is device-neutral. The surface, the audio engine and the I/O all plug into that model, and none of them assumes a particular desk. Real consoles can be attached through adapters, but they are one optional control path, not the product.
s1.p2: The server holds that state authoritatively. Clients ask for changes and render what comes back; nothing else holds an opinion about what the desk is. This matters more than it sounds. A limit that lives in a client — a channel cap, a permitted range, a safety interlock — is advisory, and the next client walks straight past it. A limit that lives at the door applies to everything that knocks.
s1.p3: Every client is a remote client. A laptop at front of house has exactly the same standing as a tablet on the wing or a phone on stage. Keeping them all looking at the same desk is not a feature of the product; it is the product.
s1.oneStream: // one stream for the whole desk

s2.title: Every fact has an address, and the address has a grammar.
s2.p1: The console publishes about eighty-five entities, and every one of them is reachable at a path built from the same grammar: {grammar}. {kind} and {index} are two segments and never one, so an address stays typeable and {curl} stays a usable acceptance test. A console you cannot address by hand is a console you cannot debug at three in the afternoon with doors at seven.
s2.p2: Each entity answers GET, PATCH and OPTIONS. OPTIONS is the contract: the writable fields, the ranges, the units and the enumerated options are published by the server, so a client renders the limits the wire sent it rather than carrying its own copy of them.

kinds.title: Kinds, not separate families
kinds.p1: Buses, DCAs, mute groups and matrices are not separate address spaces. They are kinds of channel: /channel/aux/3, /channel/dca/2, /channel/muteGroup/1, /channel/main/1.
kinds.p2: Collapsing them removed most of the protocol's duplication through an addressing decision rather than a refactor, and it is why MAIN and the buses are ordinary strips with no master-only machinery behind them.

urls.title: The contract generates the URLs
urls.p1: A row does not mint its own address space and does not mint its own path. Both are derived from the contract and the console's configuration, so the shape of the API is a consequence of the declaration rather than a thing maintained alongside it.
urls.p2: The console currently registers 183 path templates, 58 of them under /channel.

declared.title: Declared means served
declared.p1: An entity that the design declares is an entity the server answers. There is no backlog of names that exist on paper and 404 on the wire, and the two directions are checked against each other automatically rather than by inspection.
declared.p2: A control nothing can name is not a small defect — it is a control that no surface, script or automation can ever reach.

s3.title: A stream is not a different resource.
s3.quote: A stream is not a different resource. It is the same resource, still being sent.
s3.p1: Any GET takes ?watch=1 and becomes a server-sent event stream. The rule under it is testable in one line: a stream on URL R emits exactly the JSON that GET R returns. There is no second schema, no event vocabulary to learn, and no chance of the two drifting apart.
s3.p2: Every stream opens with a full snapshot, so a client that has just connected and a client that has been up all night are looking at the same desk. After that, a change is a patch on a row — never a reconnect.
s3.p3: The root stream carries every committed change on one connection. That is deliberate: a browser allows only six connections to an origin, and a surface that opens a stream per panel spends them all and then queues every subsequent request forever.
s3.p4: A handful of query parameters are clamped by the server rather than trusted from the client. One of them earns its place with a measurement: asking for a reduced number of analyser bands reduces the FFT at the source instead of after the wire, which is the difference between 372 KB and about 13 KB per frame.
s3.p5: There is no WebSocket. One door, one wire, one vocabulary — and the honest counterweight, since this page is not a sales brochure: proxy buffering is the real argument against server-sent events. Its failure mode is that things work but stutter, which at least you can see.

s4.title: One declaration, both directions.
s4.p1: A resource declares four things: its identity, its one state, its writable fields, and its projection to audio. From that single declaration the system derives the read, the write, the published contract, the broadcast frame and the actuation that reaches the engine.
s4.p2: Deriving both directions from one declaration is the load-bearing choice. When the northbound and southbound halves are written separately, they agree only as long as someone keeps them agreeing — and the failure is silent, because a control that reaches nothing still reads back correctly from the model that never doubted it. Here there is no second half to forget.
s4.p3: Three rules follow from it. An actuation that reached nothing reports failure rather than success. A control sends the composed value, never a raw flag — the engine is told what the strip's gain now is, not which of six contributing reasons changed. And buses and MAIN are strips, so they travel the same path as everything else.

latch.title: Keeping a latch honest
latch.p1: For state that lives in outboard hardware, the cheapest correct answer is query and compare: ask the device what it holds, and write only on a mismatch. Blind periodic re-assertion is the fallback, used only where a device cannot be asked.
latch.p2: Querying is not merely cheaper. A blind re-assert during a show overwrites whatever someone changed at the box, so drift becomes information instead of being papered over. Two questions decide whether a control needs the care at all: does it repair itself, and would anyone at the desk find out? A fader is self-correcting and audible, so it needs neither. Phantom power and a pad are set once at soundcheck and never re-sent — which is exactly how 20 dB of pad error can survive a whole run as "that channel sounds odd".
latch.p3: The honest exception: a REAC stagebox offers no head-amp query path. There the console's record is the state rather than a cache of it, and what the console reports as applied still may not lie about that.

s5.title: One native node, not forty subprocesses.
s5.p1: The structural signal processing is one C pw_filter node per stagebox group: per-strip gain, fader, pan, polarity, summing, the EQ bank, the gate and compressor, native delay and reverb, and the analyser tap. One node, one real-time callback, one cache-friendly pass over the whole mix.
s5.p2: It replaced roughly forty pw-loopback subprocesses, for two reasons that are about cardinality rather than about PipeWire. The daemon's file-descriptor ceiling was reached around strip eleven and the graph froze. And when a real interface suspended, PipeWire fell back to its dummy driver: the whole graph sat idle, zero busy, no audio.
s5.p3: The single-node shape also wins on merit. One real-time callback has lower jitter than N separately scheduled nodes, and one node with output links binds cleanly to the sink's driver group by construction. Nodes are created when a stagebox is plugged in and destroyed when it goes; strips are added to a live node without interrupting it; and every node shares one client, so the file-descriptor cost of the entire console is a single connection.
s5.p4: Asked for a console wider than it can carry, it refuses rather than truncating. Truncating produced a mixer that reported success and then simply had no strips past the ceiling — channels that existed in the model, drew faders on the surface, and carried no audio.

kernel.title: The kernel
kernel.body: The arithmetic lives in a single header of small static inline functions with no PipeWire, no allocation, and no libc beyond <math.h>. That is deliberate. A pan law is the kind of thing that has to be provably correct, so it is kept testable in isolation from the filter's life cycle.

realtime.title: The real-time contract
realtime.body: The callback reads per-strip parameters word-atomically, takes the strip count with an acquire, allocates nothing, logs nothing, and ramps every gain change so a moved control cannot click.

onTop.title: On top of it
onTop.body: LV2 and CLAP plugin inserts are racked in that node through one CLAP host, an LV2 plugin through the adapter libomx-clap-lv2, per strip and per output. Two layers of signal processing, and they are not interchangeable: one is the desk, the other is what you rack into it.

s6.title: The signal processing is checked against arithmetic.
s6.p1: The C core is verified by closed-form oracles: every expected value is worked out on paper first, never captured from a run of the code. The distinction is the entire point. A test that records what the implementation produced and then checks the implementation still produces it will agree with a bug forever. A test that names 500.0 ms before anything runs cannot.
s6.p2: The oracle suite is plain C with no PipeWire and no allocation, so it compiles and runs in seconds and is safe to run beside a live console.
s6.p3: Above it, controls that claim to affect audio are verified by measuring audio — a tone through a real graph, and a reading at the other end — not by asserting that a model changed. A model is correct in exactly the cases where it is the thing that is wrong.
s6.p4: A test that needs a real graph gets one of its own. Each test process starts a private PipeWire daemon in a scratch directory, on a socket named after the process, and points both the daemon and its clients at that socket rather than at the session's — so a suite cannot reach the live audio, two suites running at once cannot see each other, and nothing survives the process that made it. The daemon is not waited for by a sleep: it counts as up when it answers a question.

oracle.title: What an oracle looks like — the delay line
oracle.i1: A quarter note at 120 BPM is 500.0 ms. Not approximately: the test names 500.0, and 250.0 for an eighth, and 166.6667 for a triplet.
oracle.i2: At full wet with no feedback, an impulse at sample 0 must reappear at sample 100 with value 1.0, and sample 0 must read exactly 0.0.
oracle.i3: At feedback 0.5, the echoes at frames 10, 20 and 30 must read 1.0, 0.5 and 0.25 — the second is fb¹, the third is fb².
oracle.i4: At mix 0 the output must be bit-identical to the dry signal. Exact equality, not a tolerance.
oracle.i5: Absurd feedback of 5.0 must clamp, and stay bounded over 64 frames.
oracle.note: The same discipline covers the summing bus, the pan law, the routing matrix, the alignment fit and the recorder's file format.

lowest.title: Lowest buffer without an xrun
lowest.lede: A buffer is the short block of audio a host processes at a time, counted in frames. The host must finish each block before the next one is due; if it does not, the sound glitches, and that glitch is an xrun. The smaller the buffer, the less time audio waits before it comes out, so a smaller buffer is a lower latency. seo.title: Connecting a Control{'|'}24 — OpenMixer
seo.description: How a Digidesign Control{'|'}24 talks over Ethernet (DigiNet, EtherType 0x885F, no IP), what the network has to give it, and how to install libdiginet and diginet-probe.

hero.title: Connecting a Digidesign Control{'|'}24.
hero.lede: The Control{'|'}24 and the ProControl talk to their host over Ethernet, in a protocol of their own called DigiNet. libdiginet is a library that speaks it. This page says what the desk needs from the network and how to install the library and its test tool.

wire.title: What DigiNet is on the wire.
wire.p1: DigiNet is not IP. Every frame is a raw Ethernet II frame with EtherType 0x885F: no IP address, no DHCP, no port number. The desk is known by its MAC address, which starts with Digidesign's prefix 00:a0:7e.
wire.p2: An idle desk broadcasts an announce to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff about every 7 seconds, with its name (CNTRL{'|'}24 on a Control{'|'}24) and its firmware version. A host answers it, and from then on every frame is unicast between the desk's MAC and the host's MAC: faders, keys, lamps, displays, meters, and the acknowledgements and keepalives that hold the session up.
wire.p3: The 7-second interval and a port at 10 Mbit/s half duplex were measured on a ProControl, the Control{'|'}24's sibling of the same generation. A modern network card cabled straight to the desk may not settle on that link mode, and a cheap unmanaged 10/100 switch between the two does.

share.title: It can share a network with the web UI.
share.p1: A switch forwards a DigiNet frame like any other Ethernet frame, so the desk can sit on the same segment as the tablets and laptops that open the web UI. Machines that speak only IP ignore an EtherType they do not know. Apart from the desk's broadcast announce, a switch delivers DigiNet frames only to the console host's port, because they are addressed to its MAC.
share.p2: The frames are small: libdiginet puts at most 48 commands and 314 bytes in one, and paces display writes 2 ms apart.

segment.head: The same layer-2 segment, with no router in between.
segment.body: DigiNet has no IP header, so a router has nothing to route. The desk and the console host must be on the same Ethernet segment: one cable, or switches only.

vlan.head: The untagged (native) VLAN of the host's port.
vlan.body: The desk sends plain frames with no VLAN tag. Put it on the untagged VLAN of the switch port the host is on, and use the host's plain interface, not a VLAN sub-interface.

wired.head: A cable from the desk to the host.
wired.body: Some Wi-Fi bridges and range extenders forward only IP and ARP and drop an EtherType they do not know. Keep the path from the desk to the host wired. Web UI clients on Wi-Fi are fine: they talk IP to the console.

reac.head: Not on the REAC stagebox link.
reac.body: The interface that carries the REAC stageboxes carries their audio and nothing else. The desk goes on another interface of the host.

security.title: Security.
security.p1: DigiNet has no authentication. The desk takes a session with whichever host answers its announce, with no password and no key, and nothing in a frame proves who sent it.
security.p2: On a network you control, that is enough. On a venue LAN shared with other people, give the desk and the console host a segment of their own: a separate switch, or a VLAN that only the two of them are on.
security.p3: The desk also accepts a family of system messages (F0 13 xx 70 …) that writes to its own memory. libdiginet refuses to send it.

install.title: Install.
install.intro: libdiginet is in the FreeMixer package repositories: RPMs for Fedora (x86_64, aarch64) and DEBs for Debian bookworm and trixie (amd64, arm64). Add the repository as on the other pages and install diginet-tools, which brings the library with it.
install.pkgLib: The protocol library and its transport: discovery, the session handshake, acknowledgements, keepalive and retransmit.
install.pkgTools: diginet-probe, the command-line tool for testing a desk.
install.pkgDevel: Headers, pkg-config files and the protocol grammar, for building a program on the library.
install.caps: diginet-probe opens a packet socket, and that needs one capability, cap_net_raw. The package sets it on /usr/bin/diginet-probe when it installs, so the probe runs as your own user, not as root. A copy you build yourself has no capability until you run setcap cap_net_raw=ep on it, and again after every rebuild.
install.firstLook: With the desk cabled and powered on, the first look sends nothing: it only listens for the announce. The probe then wakes the desk, moves fader 1, lights a lamp, writes a scribble strip, logs every key and touch, and ends with a summary.
install.listen: listen only: the desk's announce, about every 7 seconds
install.probe: wake the desk and run the first test
install.probeDoc: Every option and exit status of the probe: docs/probe.md. The protocol as it is known, with a source for every claim: docs/protocol.md.

status.p1: The library is released: it holds the protocol, the transport and the probe.

seo.title: Getting started — OpenMixer
seo.description: From a built checkout to one channel audible in the main mix: start the server and the surface, patch an input, and hear it.

hero.title: From nothing to one channel in the mix.
hero.lede: Everything below assumes a built checkout — see Get it if you have not built one yet. This chapter does one job: start the console, patch one real input, and hear it at MAIN. Once that works, the rest of the manual is about everything OpenMixer can do beyond it.

code.fromTop: From the top of a built checkout — see Get it if you have not built one yet.
code.secondTerminal: In a second terminal, the surface:
code.thirdTerminal: From a third terminal, at any point — this is what "in the mix" means on the wire.

s1.title: Start the console and the surface.
s1.p1: Two processes, two terminals. The server is the console — it owns the mix and needs no configuration file to come up. The surface is a plain web page; nothing about it is privileged over any other client that will later connect to the same server.
s1.p2: The dev server prints the address to open — typically http://localhost:3000. The surface does not hardcode the console's address: it discovers the endpoint from the origin that served it, so the same build works from a phone on the same network without being rebuilt for it.

s2.title: Check the header before you touch a fader.
s2.p1: Open the page. The connection indicator in the header says whether you are looking at the live console or the offline fallback — a simulated board the surface shows itself when no server answers, precisely so the controls can be learned with nothing behind them. If you expected a live desk and moving a fader does nothing, this is almost always the reason: check the indicator before assuming anything else is broken.

s3.title: Patch a real input onto channel 1.
s3.p1: The channel roster already exists — a console's strip count is fixed at boot, and channel 1 is there whether or not anything feeds it. What it hears is a separate fact: open the patchbay and connect a real source — the first input of a plain USB interface is enough, a stagebox is not required — to channel 1's input. Nothing else needs creating first.

s4.title: Bring the channel up and send it to MAIN.
s4.p1: On channel 1: make sure it is not muted, and bring the fader up towards unity. Every channel sums into MAIN by default, so there is no separate routing step for this — the meter on channel 1 and the meter on MAIN should move together as soon as there is signal on the patched input. If MAIN moves but you hear nothing, the fault is downstream of the console — MAIN's own output patch, or whatever MAIN is patched to.

s5.title: Verify it without your ears, if you want to be sure.
s5.p1: The console is addressable by hand, on purpose. This reads the exact fader you just moved, straight from the server:
s5.p2: {position} is the 0–1 value the fader cap sits at; {db} is what that position means in gain. Add {watch} to follow it live instead of reading it once — the full address space is in the {link}.

seo.description: Memory, CPU, context switches and xruns of a chain of omx plugins hosted in one worker or in one process per plugin, measured on a Raspberry Pi 5.

hero.title: One worker per chain, or one process per plugin.
hero.lede: plugin-hostd can run a chain of plugins inside one worker process, or give every plugin its own process. This page is one measurement of the two on a Raspberry Pi 5, with every row, and with what was not measured.

result.title: What came out.
result.rss: Memory: with 16 plugins, resident memory (RSS) is 14x smaller grouped (125.4 MB against 1764.6 MB at 48 kHz) and proportional memory (PSS) is 2.8x smaller (42.9 MB against 118.2 MB).
result.cpu: CPU: 1.2 to 1.9x less when grouped, across 3, 8 and 16 plugins at 48 and 96 kHz.
result.ctx: Context switches: up to about 14x fewer when grouped, 13.9x at 48 kHz and 14.8x at 96 kHz with 16 plugins.
result.xruns: Xruns over the 12 runs of each mode: 10 grouped against 41 with one process per plugin.
result.why: RSS counts a shared library once for every process that maps it, so a design with many processes looks larger than it is. PSS divides shared pages between the processes that use them, so it is the honest figure, and both are shown. Do not read the RSS ratio as the saving in real memory.
result.xrunCaveat: Each run is one window of 10 seconds and the xruns in it are few and unevenly spread, so the 10 against 41 is suggestive and not proof. Read it as a count and not as a rate.

method.title: How it was measured.
method.setup: Raspberry Pi 5 with 4 cores running Zynthian, CPU governor on performance during the runs. plugin-hostd 0.12.0 with omx-clap-host 0.22.1 as the worker. N instances of omx plugins in series (chorus, comp, deesser, delay, drive, eq8, flanger and geq, in turn), a sine in, 256 frames, on a private JACK server with a dummy driver. The JACK server of the live system was not touched. Both modes produce the same output signal (peaks equal within 1%).
method.window: Each run is one window of 10 seconds after 1 second of warm-up. N is 3, 8 or 16, the rate 48 or 96 kHz, each with and without stress (8 busy-loop processes on the 4 cores). That is 12 runs of each mode.
method.columns: Memory and CPU are summed over plugin-hostd and its workers. CPU is a percentage of one core. Context switches are voluntary plus involuntary ones of all their threads in the window. DSP is the JACK load, average and maximum, read once a second. Xruns are the JACK xrun callbacks in the window.

notMeasured.title: What was not measured.
notMeasured.frames: Only 256 frames. 128 frames were not run.
notMeasured.hosts: Only plugin-hostd, with omx plugins. No other plugin host, and no third-party plugin, is in these numbers.
notMeasured.planner: The grouping planner that will decide which plugins share a worker is not part of this result. The numbers compare the two fixed modes and no default has been changed because of them.
notMeasured.hardware: DSP load and xruns are those of the JACK dummy driver. No claim about real audio hardware is made.

ratios.title: The ratios.
ratios.intro: One process per plugin divided by grouped, without stress. Processes are shown as individual / grouped. For CPU and context switches a ratio above 1 means the grouped run used less.

raw.intro: The 24 runs as measured. Memory in MB, CPU as percent of one core, DSP as average / maximum percent.

seo.title: Undo and the history — OpenMixer
seo.description: The console’s journal: one list of changes for the whole desk, undo and redo, reverting one change out of the middle, and the offer you get when the field has moved since.

hero.title: One list of what changed, for the whole desk.
hero.lede: The console keeps a journal of the changes made to it: one entry per gesture, in plain sentences, with who made it and when. Ctrl+Z walks back through it, and any single entry can be taken back on its own without disturbing the ones after it. What the journal deliberately does not hold is as important as what it does.

fader.note: A fader move. One drag is one entry, not forty.

phantom.note: A discrete change: the two values are the words the control uses.

send.note: A send names both ends, because “send” alone would not say which.

paste.note: One gesture that touched eight strips is one entry, and reverts as one.

order.note: A reorder has no before-and-after worth printing, so it prints neither.

never.cue: Cue, the monitor, talkback and dim.

s1.title: One console, one journal.
s1.p1: The journal belongs to the desk, not to your screen. Every surface writing to the console — the laptop at front of house, the tablet on the wing, a control surface, a script — appends to the same list, so your Ctrl+Z can walk back the change somebody else just made.
s1.p2: That is the point rather than a hazard, and the list is what makes it safe: each entry says where it came from before you press anything. An entry made on a surface names the surface, one made by a REST client names the client’s address, and an entry that is itself an undo says that too.
s1.p3: It holds the last 512 changes and the panel says so at the foot of the list. The bound is a count and not a span of time, because a quiet passage should not cost you the history of the noisy one before it.
s1.p4: The journal is not saved. It lives for as long as the console is running, and a restart starts a fresh one — an entry remembers what a field read a moment ago, which is a claim only the running process can make honestly.

s2.title: What an entry says.
s2.p1: An entry is one sentence: what was changed, then what it read before and what it reads now. Channels are named the way the rest of the desk names them — CH3, Aux2, Main — levels carry one decimal, and a switch reads on or off.
s2.p2: A drag is one entry. While you are moving a fader the console keeps folding the movement into the entry it already opened, keeping the value you started from and the value you are at now, and seals it half a second after you stop. Two separate nudges a second apart are two entries, and CH3’s fader never folds into CH4’s.
s2.p3: The sentence is built on your screen, in your language, from a change the console describes rather than a phrase it writes — so the same entry reads as a sentence in Catalan, Spanish or English depending on who is looking at it.

s3.title: Undo, redo, and where the cursor sits.
s3.p1: The undo and redo buttons live in the header, and each one names what it would hit before you press it — Undo: CH3 fader rather than an arrow with no object. The keys are Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z and Ctrl+Y, and they do nothing while you are typing in a field.
s3.p2: Undo and redo move a cursor through the one list; they do not add to it. Entries below the cursor are the ones the desk is currently sounding; entries above it are undone and stay in the list, dimmed and struck through, because redo is one press away. The foot of the panel counts how many are in that state.
s3.p3: Making any new change from an undone position drops the undone entries — the ordinary rule, and the reason the panel shows them struck through rather than hiding them: you can see what you are about to lose.

s4.title: Taking back one change out of the middle.
s4.p1: Every entry in the list carries an Undo this button. It writes exactly one field — the one that entry addressed — back to the value the entry started from. Nothing else moves. Move a fader, mute another channel, pan a third, then take back the fader: the fader returns and the mute and the pan stay where they are.
s4.p2: A revert is a change like any other, so it appends its own entry, marked as having come from the history rather than from a surface. The list grows by one; it never rewrites itself.
s4.p3: There is no entry in the list you cannot take back. Anything that must never be replayed never became an entry in the first place — which is the next section.

s5.title: When the field has moved since.
s5.p1: An entry can be minutes old, and in that time somebody else — or a later gesture of your own — may have moved the same control. Taking the entry back would then jump the field from a value nobody expects to another value nobody asked for, so the console asks first:
s5.quote: This has changed since — db reads −3.0 now, not the −12.0 this step left (changed by entry 47).
s5.p2: Go back anyway makes the write. Leave it does nothing. Both the header’s buttons and the list’s rows draw the offer in space they already reserve, so nothing under your finger moves when it appears. A jump-back taken from a row in the list records in its new entry that it went over the later one, so the list says a jump-back happened and what it jumped over.
s5.p3: Ctrl+Z asks the same question. The top of the list is compared before it is replayed, exactly as a row in the list is compared when you click it, and redo compares the value its own undo left standing. One question, three doors: if the field still reads what the step left, the walk goes through without a word; if it does not, you get the offer and nothing is written until you answer it.
s5.p4: The console never takes that decision for you and never retries behind your back. If the desk moves again while the question is on screen, the offer is dropped rather than answered against a value that has gone stale.

s6.title: What the journal never holds.
s6.p1: The gig-safety controls are not in the list at all. No entry, no address, no refusal — the list simply never mentions them:
s6.p2: A list with a per-entry revert is a more dangerous thing than a single Ctrl+Z: it can reach back past everything that happened since. Undoing a spare swap puts a dead microphone back on a channel; undoing a mute opens one you closed for a reason. These controls are one press to set and one press to clear, and that is the whole recovery they need.
s6.p3: Changes the console makes on its own account are also absent — recalling a scene, loading a session, healing a route, a control surface re-driving itself. The list is what people did to the desk.
s6.p4: Meters, RTA and telemetry never appear: they are measurements, not settings.

s7.title: What empties it.
s7.p1: Loading a show empties the journal, and so does anything else that restates the desk wholesale: recalling a scene, loading a session or a patch, applying a channel config, saving or deleting one, and resizing the console. After one of those the list starts again from empty.
s7.p2: That is deliberate. Those actions rewrite hundreds of facts at once, and a list that offered to take one of them back out of the middle would be offering something it cannot honestly do. The way back from a load is the autosave the console takes before it, which is its own mechanism.
s7.foot: The list itself is {history}, the cursor is {cursor}, and a single entry is taken back at {revert}. All three doors — that one and {undo} and {redo} — take the same {override} argument, and every fire spells it out: a client that has to write {false} cannot mean {true} by accident. Fields, ranges and the refusals each can send back are in the {rest} and the {codes}.

seo.title: The MCP server — OpenMixer
seo.description: An MCP server over stdio that lets a coding agent read and write a running console through the console’s own contract, and read the contracts its DSP stages declare.

install.top: From the top of the workspace.
install.stdio: stdio; an MCP client starts it and speaks to it over the pipe.

skills.design-first: Resolve the governing design before reading or writing a line. It is three questions — which primitive does this belong to, does it need a new word in the vocabulary, and why is it not an existing thing configured differently — and a search of the specs and the log for the subject before anything is built. The week that produced it lost most of its time re-deriving decisions that were already written down.
skills.design-ruling: Record a decision where the automation reads it. When a spec is written or amended, a contract field changes, or a law is superseded, the ruling goes into the design records and the spec map that the pre-edit gate consults — otherwise the next person to touch that file is told the old law.
skills.false-signals: The house rule for a signal that does not observe what it claims to. A green suite over an empty function body, a grep that finds nothing because it is broken, a probe that reports silence because it was pointed at the wrong strip: each one has cost a night here. The rule it enforces is to prove a check can detect presence before believing its report of absence.
skills.round-trip-proof: A feature is done when the operator’s whole job has been measured end to end, not when its parts pass. It is the skill to read before calling anything finished, and the one that governs any audio measurement that comes back a null, a ratio or a surprise — a gain test needs a real signal well above the noise floor before its delta means anything.
skills.openmixer-dev-discipline: The house style, in one place: how a change lands in git, what the TypeScript and C look like, the rules for the surface’s components and its translations, which testing tier a change owes, and how the packaging stays parametrised. Its first principle is operator authority — the console states the cost of a choice and lets the operator make it, rather than vetoing; the narrow exception is anything irreversible that lands on people who are not at the desk.
skills.lane-discipline: How parallel work stays separable. Each lane gets its own worktree and branch, commits often with explicit paths, keeps its evidence in the repository rather than in a scratch file, and never merges its own work onto the integration branch. Written after a fan-out lost a night of findings that existed only outside the repository.
skills.settle-gate: The procedure that puts an integration branch on the live console. It is deliberately not something a lane can invoke: it builds before it deploys, verifies with a question only the new commit can answer rather than with a health check, and drops real audio if it is wrong.

hero.title: A console an agent can read and write through the contract every other client uses.
hero.lede: OpenMixer ships an MCP server over stdio. Its tools read and write a running console through the console’s own REST contract, and read the contracts each channel stage declares at the moment they are asked. It decides nothing: every answer is data the desk or the tree already holds, named with where it came from.

s1.title: Running it.
s1.p1: It is a workspace package, {'@'}openmixer/mcp-server, and it speaks MCP over stdio — an MCP client starts the process and talks to it over the pipe. There is no port, no daemon and nothing to leave running.
s1.p2: The server walks up from its working directory to the workspace root and reads the contracts of that tree, so a second checkout answers with its own declarations and nothing is bundled into the package.

s2.title: {count} tools, in two families.
s2.p1: One family is the REST entity door as it stands: the roster, a row, its declared travels, one frame of a metered row, and a write. The other reads the contracts a channel’s DSP stages declare: the laws, the parameters and their limits. The table below is generated from the package’s registered tool table, not written by hand, and the package’s own test refuses a description that has drifted from the registry.

s3.title: One tool writes, and it writes once.
s3.p1: Every tool but one reads. console_patch sends a real write to a real desk, so it sends exactly one request, never retries it, and hands back the console’s status, its Allow header and its body as they arrived. A refusal is the desk’s ruling and is returned verbatim rather than interpreted, which is the same contract every other client works under: the console decides, and what comes back is what it decided.
s3.p2: The tool holds nothing back on its own account. A write that fires an operation the console’s own confirms sheet gates — a channel-config apply that would move gain, trim or pan is the example — is sent, and the console refuses it with CONFIRM_REQUIRED while the preview lists moves and the operator’s sign-off is on. The refusal comes back with the preview in the body, like any other answer. Calling again with confirm: true — which rides the delta as the row’s own confirm argument — applies it, because the agent has now been shown what it is agreeing to. The gate is the desk’s, so an agent, a browser and an OSC surface are refused identically and answer identically; there is no client-side policy to keep in step.
s3.p3: The metered row is the one place a read is not simply a GET. A pump-fed row measures only while something is watching it, so an unmeasured frame is followed by a single watch that closes the moment the first measured frame lands. No stream is left open.
s3.p4: The tools stand on a fake console with the real console’s shapes, checked across the wire on values rather than on shapes — a −20 dBFS reading has to decode to −20. A live desk is not part of that suite.

s4.title: The process skills the tree carries.
s4.p1: Alongside the server, the repository keeps its working discipline as readable documents, one per subject, checked in beside the code they govern. Each one exists because something went wrong the other way. They are listed here because they describe how this project is built, not because a reader needs to run them.
s4.p2: The repository is not public yet, so these documents live in a tree you cannot clone today. They are named rather than summarised away, because a name is what makes the description checkable the day it opens.

seo.title: Plugins and the insert rack — OpenMixer
seo.description: Racking LV2 plugins on a channel or a bus, where they sit in the signal, what mono and stereo mean here, the latency budget by destination, and the two refusals you will meet.

hero.title: Racking a plugin, and what the desk checks before it lets you.
hero.lede: OpenMixer hosts LV2 plugins on channels and on bus outputs. Everything the desk itself does — EQ, gate, compressor, delay, reverb, buses, routing — is native and needs nothing installed; plugins are what you add on top. The console decides two things for you before a rack lands: whether the plugin fits the strip’s width, and whether the destination can afford the delay it adds.

places.title: Two places a plugin can sit.
places.rack: The rack is the list of plugins on the way out of the strip, after the fader and before the bus. It is the ordinary one: open the Plugins tab on the processing view, or the plugin rack pane, press add, pick a plugin, and it appears as the next slot.
places.chain: The chain is the strip’s own structure — trim, EQ, gate, fader — and it offers named points inside that structure where one plugin can be placed: Top-Of-Ch, Post-Trim, Pre-EQ, Post-EQ and Pre-Fader. Use it when the plugin has to run before something the console does natively rather than after everything.
places.bus: On a bus, the rack is the output rack: crossover, limiter, output EQ — the loudspeaker management for what leaves the desk on that output.

slots.title: Slots, order and bypass.
slots.slot: A slot is a position in the rack, not a fixed bay: there is no such thing as an empty slot, only a shorter rack. Drag to reorder, or use the arrows; the × removes a plugin; the bypass toggle passes the signal through it untouched. A bypassed plugin is still loaded and still owns its delay, which is why the rack shows its latency whether it is bypassed or not — and why un-bypassing is judged exactly like adding it back.
slots.remove: Removing a plugin bypasses it, unlinks it and retires its slot: the strip is fed straight through before anything else happens, and the console never hands that instance out again. What it does not do is give the instance back to the plugin host — the host cannot free one without falling over, so an un-racked plugin sits on the graph, silent and unlinked, until the host next starts. The host has 9991 instance slots and they are never recycled inside one run, so this is an accounting fact rather than a daily one; if you ever do reach the end of them, the console says exactly that and names how many un-racked plugins are holding the rest:
slots.full: the plugin host has no instance slot left (9991 in all, 9803 of them held by un-racked plugins it cannot free) — restart the plugin host to reclaim them
slots.oneList: The rack itself is one list, and every edit is that list rewritten: adding, removing, reordering and swapping a slot for another plugin all go through the same door, so there is one place a rack can be judged and one place it can be refused.
slots.latency: Each slot shows the plugin’s measured latency in milliseconds, and the rack shows the total at the foot, with the console’s own verdict on it underneath. A verdict that has not arrived yet shows nothing under the total, never a false fine.

picker.title: What is in the picker.
picker.lists: The picker lists LV2 plugins that are both installed on this machine and in the console’s curated palette, grouped by the job they do rather than by vendor. The palette exists so the list is a short, sensible one instead of six hundred raw plugin identifiers; a plugin the machine does not have drops out of it rather than sitting there as a dead entry.
picker.empty: On a fresh machine the picker is empty. That is expected: nothing about the desk depends on a plugin being installed.
picker.chips: Each entry carries two chips. One is its latency class — zero or low, high, or not measured — and a plugin that is not for live use says so regardless of its figure. The other is how its family stands: the plugin sets behave differently enough that the family is worth knowing before you commit a channel to one.
picker.narrowed: The list is not the same on every strip. The strip’s own rack door publishes what it will accept here, narrowed by the same width test the refusal below uses, and the picker greys everything that is not on that list rather than letting you pick it and then reading the refusal. The narrowing is worked out each time you ask, from the strip’s width as it is at that moment, so making a strip stereo makes the stereo plugins pickable with no reload. A plugin whose leg count the catalog does not know is offered rather than hidden — the desk does not refuse on a fact it does not have.

width.title: Mono and stereo: a plugin wider than the strip is refused.
width.knows: The desk already knows the strip’s width — mono or stereo, from what is patched into it — and the catalog already knows how many audio legs a plugin puts out. A mono plugin on a stereo strip is fine. A stereo plugin on a mono strip is refused:
width.refusal: http://lsp-plug.in/plugins/lv2/para_equalizer_x16_stereo has 2 audio legs and this strip is mono — rack the plugin’s mono build, or make the strip stereo.
width.why: It is a refusal rather than a fold because folding it would be silent and wrong. Both of the plugin’s output legs land in the strip’s one input port and are summed there, which is a measured 6.02 dB lift on the main mix with no control touched — a stereo EQ at unity, doing nothing, making the channel twice as loud. The mono twin of the same plugin moves the main mix by 0.00 dB.
width.whole: The whole rack is refused, not silently trimmed, and the refusal names the first plugin that does not fit. A plugin whose leg count the catalog does not know is not a finding and refuses nothing.
width.other: The other refusal you can meet is about the point rather than the width:
width.postFader: a plugin cannot run at Post-Fader yet — rack it at one of Top-Of-Ch, Post-Trim, Pre-EQ, Post-EQ, Pre-Fader instead.
width.deliberate: Post-Fader is a real point on the chain and the slot for it is deliberately still there, because a missing mechanism you can see is better than one that has been tidied away. Until it carries audio, the console greys the control and says so rather than accepting a rack that would never run. Nothing is written when either refusal fires.

budget.title: The latency budget, by where the signal is going.
budget.intro: Delay that is unremarkable on a reverb send is unusable on a wedge, so the budget is a property of the destination rather than of the plugin. A monitor destination is held to 5 ms and the edit is refused if the chain exceeds it; a program destination has 100 ms and an effects destination 60 ms, and both of those warn — the edit lands and the finding rides along with it. Every figure names the sample rate it was judged at.

within.text: This chain uses 2.1 ms of the 5.0 ms budget at 48000 Hz (2.9 ms left).
within.note: Carried so the rack can show headroom, not only trouble.

over.text: ZaMaximX2 puts this chain at 7.4 ms — over the 5.0 ms budget for a monitor destination at 48000 Hz. On a monitor send the performer hears themself that late.
over.note: On a monitor destination this refuses the edit; nothing is applied.

mayExceed.text: Calf Limiter has parameter-dependent latency: this chain is now between 3.0 and 12.0 ms against a 5.0 ms budget at 48000 Hz. Check the look-ahead before the show.
mayExceed.note: A look-ahead you can turn up past the limit later in the day.

unknown.text: Dragonfly Hall has no measured latency at 96000 Hz, so this chain’s total is unknown — the 1.8 ms shown counts only what could be resolved.
unknown.note: Never counted as zero, and never quietly a pass.

budget.refused: When the budget refuses, the write comes back as the destination cannot afford this insert chain, carrying the finding above as its reason. Latency adds up across the whole chain, a bypassed slot costs nothing, and a plugin whose delay could not be resolved at this rate is never counted as zero.
budget.row: The verdict is also a row you can simply read, at any time, without making an edit: it answers whether this channel’s destination can afford the rack it is carrying right now. Before it existed the only way to learn that a re-clocked graph had pushed a chain over its budget was for the next edit to fail.

editor.title: The editor, and what a control is showing you.
editor.panel: Selecting a slot opens a control panel built entirely from what the plugin declares about itself — one control per parameter, each choosing its own kind of widget. There is no hand-written panel per plugin, which is why an eleven-parameter compressor and a hundred-and-eighty-parameter EQ both open. The grid never scrolls; the panel sizes itself to the number of parameters. Its header carries the plugin name and a bypass toggle, so A/B is one press, and an EQ-role plugin also gets a response curve.
editor.ranges: The ranges, defaults, units and named steps those controls bind come from the console, not from the browser: the desk serves the descriptor it scanned on its own machine for the plugin in the open slot, and the panel is drawn from that. It matters because the same plugin identifier can be a different build on a different rig, and a knob drawn at another machine’s range would send values this one never accepts. The copy shipped with the interface is used only where no desk has answered — offline, in the mock, in the first moment before the row lands.
editor.defaults: A plugin the console has not been told to change shows the plugin’s own default, which is a fact about the plugin and not a reading from it. The host cannot be asked what a control is at this instant, so what the desk shows is what it commanded; a value it never commanded is a placeholder.
editor.session: Parameter values, bypass state, the selected preset and the order of the rack are all part of the session, so a saved show comes back with its racks as they were.

arriving.title: What this chapter does not describe yet.
arriving.postFader: Post-Fader as a working insert point on the chain. When it carries audio, it joins the list the refusal above prints and both stop firing, with no change to anything that talks to the console.

declare.title: The plugin declares itself.

layout.title: omx-panel lays it out.
layout.text: It orders the controls into sections, gives each a role, picks the family the controls make together and cuts the pages of eight a controller shows. When the plugin declares a panel of its own, that panel wins.

write.text: For MOD and Zynthian it writes a MOD GUI into the plugin's LV2 bundle: modgui.ttl and a modgui/ directory. A toggle becomes a switch, a choice or a short integer travel a selector, and every other travel a knob.

hero.title: Plugins from your distribution, and what the console does with them.
hero.lede: The console runs LV2 and CLAP plugins that were not written for it. Each one runs in a process of its own, and each can be measured before a show, so you know in advance whether it is safe to rely on.

install.intro: A third-party plugin installs like any other package. As an example, the LSP plugin suite, in its LV2 and CLAP builds:

hostd.title: How the console runs them.
hostd.workers: plugin-hostd runs LV2 and CLAP plugins, each in a worker process of its own, behind the same socket protocol the console already speaks. Audio never passes through the daemon: every worker is an audio client of its own.
hostd.crash: If a plugin crashes, only its worker is restarted, with its settings put back, and the other plugins keep playing. A plugin that keeps crashing is singled out and given up on without touching its neighbours.
hostd.pins: Before a plugin starts, the daemon checks that its files are the ones that were checked: it hashes them and compares them with the plugin's recorded pin. A plugin updated or swapped behind your back is refused until you accept the new files, so a change cannot slip in unchecked. A plugin whose record says it was refused does not start.
hostd.grouped: How much memory, CPU and how many context switches a chain in one worker saves against one process per plugin is measured on {page}.

verdicts.title: What a verdict means for you.
verdicts.intro: Four verdicts. The deciding reason is printed beside it.

suitable.text: Every check was made and passed. The plugin is safe to run inside the console's own engine process. This is the only verdict that counts as qualified.

conditional.text: It works, with a caution, for example a high cost at small buffer sizes. It is run isolated, and the reason names the caution.
conditional.do: Rack it if you can live with the reason, and read the reason first.

unknown.text: Something was not measured. An unmeasured plugin is never counted as a pass.
unknown.do: Measure it again, or leave it off the live rig.

unsuitable.text: A measured failure: a crash, a memory error in the plugin's own code, a real-time violation (it allocates memory, takes locks or makes system calls while it processes audio) or a required feature the host does not provide.
unsuitable.do: Leave it off the live rig.

verdicts.worst: The worst check decides the verdict.
verdicts.host: A verdict is judged for a particular host. The default is the console itself; the same measurements can be judged for other hosts, so a plugin can be fine in one and refused in another.

seo.title: The REAC segment role — OpenMixer
seo.description: Which end of a REAC wire the console presents as: mixer, recorder, or automatic — what each one does, what automatic decides from, and the four sentences the console gives you when it will not take a role.

hero.title: Which end of the wire the console is.
hero.lede: A REAC segment has exactly one master. Either this console masters it and drives the stageboxes, or another desk does and the console joins as the box end. That choice is the segment’s role, and it is one of two things you set per segment in Setup → Clock — the other being the rate. The default leaves the choice to the console, which observes the wire before it asserts anything.

segments.title: Segments, and the two things you set on one.
segments.p1: A segment is one REAC wire — REAC A, REAC B and so on, listed with the patch name of what is on it. Everything else the card shows is observation: what is mastering it, at what pace, which link is up, which box model and firmware answered, whether there is a conflict. Two fields are yours: the rate and the role.
segments.p2: A field you never set stays unset, and an unset field leaves the daemon’s own best default standing — which is not the same as choosing it. The one exception is the role, which behaves as automatic until you say otherwise.
segments.p3: Both picks are staged rather than sent as you scroll. You choose, then confirm, and the confirmation says what it will cost: changing a role re-establishes the segment on the wire, a few seconds of interruption. Changing the rate is worse — about six seconds while the box re-locks, and on a box carrying the PA return that is the whole rig.

roles.title: Mixer, recorder, automatic.
roles.mixer: Mixer. The console is the desk end of the pairing. It masters the segment, drives the stageboxes on it, and owns the wire’s pace — which is why the rate is only yours to set in this role.
roles.recorder: Recorder. The console presents as the box end and joins a wire another desk is mastering, to take a feed off it. It asserts no pace of its own and follows the foreign desk physically.
roles.automatic: Automatic. The default. The console reads the segment first and then takes whichever end is open: a wire with nothing mastering it, or one it is already mastering, it takes as the mixer; a wire a foreign desk is mastering, it joins as the recorder. Unplugging a desk and having the console pick the boxes up is automatic doing its job.
roles.never: Automatic never asserts against a foreign master. A desk is joined, not fought — one master per segment is REAC’s law, not a policy of this console’s. If a stagebox is mastering the wire, or if the console cannot tell what is, it asserts nothing at all and tells you why.
roles.note: The word recorder does double duty on this desk, and the labels keep the two apart. The control in Setup is called REAC role, and its three settings are Mixer, Recorder and Automatic — that recorder is the end of a REAC pairing the console presents as. Everywhere the desk means the multitrack recorder that writes takes to disk it says recorder (takes) instead, so a sentence like “this console has no recorder (takes)” is never about the wire.

watching.title: What automatic is watching, and when it decides.
watching.p1: Two facts, both published by the wire: whether the segment has a master and whether it is ours, and — when it is not ours — whether the thing mastering it is a desk, a stagebox, or something the console cannot identify. That is the whole input.
watching.p2: It is not a timer. Every segment resolves when it announces itself, so a decision follows the wire rather than a clock: a desk that arrives after the console has taken a segment is seen on its next announce and automatic re-resolves against it. A slow desk costs one re-resolution and never a fight.
watching.p3: Automatic runs on every segment the console can see, including ones you have never touched — a fresh console does not sit inert on a wire waiting to be told once.
watching.p4: The console re-asserts what you asked for, never what it worked out. Leaving a segment on automatic keeps it on automatic: an observation that changes cannot quietly write a fixed role into your show.
watching.p5: The card shows the daemon’s own answer beside the role you picked — Applied, Re-establishing…, or Hunting for a desk…. A recorder waiting on a desk that is not there reads as hunting and never as applied, which is the honest answer.

refusals.title: When the console will not take the role you asked for.
refusals.intro: It says which of four things happened, on the segment’s own card, and where there is a single gesture that resolves it, that gesture is a button beside the sentence — never a config file and never a restart.

deskMasters.when: You asked to be the mixer, and a desk already masters the wire
deskMasters.text: You asked to be the mixer, but a desk is already mastering this segment. One master per segment is REAC law, so the console is holding and has asserted nothing on the wire.
deskMasters.doing: The panel offers one button: switch this segment to recorder.

rivalBox.when: A stagebox on the segment has its Mode switch on M
rivalBox.text: A stagebox on this segment has its REAC Mode switch on M (master), so the console will not take a role beside it. Set the switch to S (slave) and power-cycle the box.
rivalBox.doing: There is no button, because the remedy is a switch on the box. Inventing a control the console cannot honour would be the other half of the same lie.

rivalUnknown.when: Something is mastering the wire and the console cannot tell what
rivalUnknown.text: Something is mastering this segment and the console cannot tell what it is, so it will not take a role beside it. Check what else is on this wire.
rivalUnknown.doing: Also no button. Find out what is on the segment first.

noMaster.when: You asked to record, and nothing is mastering the wire
noMaster.text: You asked to record, but nothing is mastering this segment. The role has been asserted and the console is hunting for a desk; until one appears there is nothing to record from.
noMaster.doing: This one has already gone to the wire — you chose it. The panel offers a switch back to mixer.

rate.title: The rate belongs to whoever masters the wire.
rate.p1: A segment following a foreign desk has no rate to set: it follows that desk’s pace, physically. The console refuses a rate write on such a segment rather than accepting one it cannot honour, and the panel says so — a slave segment has no rate to set — it follows the foreign master’s pace.
rate.p2: The gate is on what the segment is running now, not on what you intend it to become. Promoting a segment to mixer and setting its rate is therefore two confirmations, not one: take the wire first, then set the pace on it.
rate.p3: A rate the segment does not publish as drivable is refused too, naming the rates it will take. It is never quietly rounded to the nearest one it likes.

file.title: The file the console writes.
file.p1: The REAC daemon is configured by a small environment file at ~/.config/openmixer/reac.env, and the console generates it: setting the role in Setup is what puts REAC_ROLE on disk, so the choice survives a restart of the daemon and of the machine. The write is atomic — a new file is put in place whole — so an interrupted save never leaves a half-written configuration behind.
file.p2: The file says what the console is on the wire, and holds nothing else: the role, the two interfaces, the mixer family and the wire’s rate, plus the box model where the rig still carries an expectation of one. Which stagebox is actually out there is learned from the wire and is deliberately not written down here.
file.p3: Because the console regenerates the file rather than editing it in place, it is the console’s file and not a shared one: a comment or a variable of your own added by hand is dropped the next time the console writes it. Keep anything you need for yourself somewhere else.
file.p4: The console is conservative about writing at all. A role change writes only when the file actually says something different, and if there is no file, or the file does not parse, nothing is written — an unconfigured host stays unconfigured rather than acquiring a binding nobody chose.

arriving.title: What this chapter does not describe yet.
arriving.rateControl: A rate control that hides itself on a following segment. The panel decides whether to offer it from the role you asked for rather than from the role the segment is running, so on a segment left on automatic that has joined a foreign desk the control can still be there. The write is refused honestly if you use it, with the sentence above — nothing is set behind your back.

seo.title: Recording and the virtual soundcheck — OpenMixer
seo.description: Arming channels, which taps a channel records, the take library, exporting the print of the main mix, and running a virtual soundcheck: load, engage, play, eject.

hero.title: Capture a show, then mix it again without the band.
hero.lede: Multitrack recording and virtual soundcheck work: their first real take on the rig was eighty-four tracks, and they have not yet carried a show. What is described below is what the console does today; anything still being built is marked as such at the end of the chapter.

captures.title: What a take captures.
captures.default: There is no channel picker to fill in before you record. Every patched input and MAIN are armed by default, and you opt a channel out rather than opting channels in — a channel with nothing patched to it records nothing worth keeping, so the console leaves it out of the derivation without changing what you asked for: patch something into it later and it arms again, with no extra step. Aux and matrix channels are not armed unless you ask for them.
captures.patched: Patched means the signal actually arrives, not that the patch list says it should. The console asks the audio graph whether a link runs from the source into that strip’s input, and a strip whose patch has not been made — a stagebox that has not turned up, a device the graph has not offered yet — is left out of the take even though the desk shows it patched. That distinction was bought the hard way: a take of eighty-four tracks in which one channel’s two files were 94-byte headers, found the next morning.
captures.omissions: So the console says what it is not recording, once, at the moment the take starts and the arm set becomes unchangeable: the channels it left out are named in the console’s log, with the reason — a declared source with no link into the strip’s input. They are also missing from the armed count you can read while the take runs, and the take itself carries no track for them. A running take reports the omissions it started with and does not re-derive them, so linking a strip mid-show never makes it look as though a take could have carried it.
captures.taps: Each armed channel is captured at two points by default — its raw input, taken straight after the trim, and its post-fader signal — so a re-mix afterwards has both the untouched source and what you actually pushed to the house that night. An input channel is offered a third point, pre-fader, and the three are a set rather than a choice: a channel can record pre and post fader at the same time. A bus master is offered one point, post-fader, and that is a stated fact about a bus rather than an oversight.
captures.tapsFixed: Which taps a channel records is decided when the take starts. Changing the set while a take is running moves nothing and costs nothing — it is a decision about the files the next take will open.
captures.setFixed: The channel set is fixed for the whole take. Arming or unarming a channel while a take is running does nothing to that take — the set was decided the moment it started, on purpose: a capture that could gain a track mid-show is one where nobody can say afterwards what the first ten minutes actually held.

recording.title: Recording a take.
recording.transport: Each channel strip carries a record control showing whether that channel is armed. Recording itself is a console-wide transport, not a per-channel one: start it and every currently-armed channel begins together; stop it and the take becomes part of the library.
recording.refuses: Starting refuses rather than half-starting: with nothing armed, with a take already running, or with less disk space than the take needs to open safely, the console says so before the first sample rather than leaving you with a folder to clean up. The refusal names the numbers — how much space it wanted and how much there was — because "not enough space" is not something you can act on and "it needs 14 GB and there is 3" is.

library.title: The take library.
library.listed: Every take that finished recording is listed, newest first, by when it started and how long it ran. There is no upload and no import — the only way a take enters the library is by being recorded — and there is deliberately no delete yet: erasing a multitrack take safely, while a render or a soundcheck might hold it open, is real work the console has not done, and a delete button that is not safe is worse than no delete button.
library.files: The files themselves are plain WAV — RF64 once a track passes 4 GB, ordinary RIFF WAV below it, and every reader treats the two the same — one mono 32-bit float file per track, at the rate the graph was running when the take was recorded.
library.legs: One file per track means one file per leg, so a stereo channel contributes two, sharing a channel and a tap between them. Each one names its side in the take's own record, left or right, so nothing downstream has to infer a stereo pair from the order the files happen to be listed in. The file names stay the track number and the tap — ch09.post-fader.wav — because that is what stops a DAW laying the wrong tap under the vocal; the side is in the record beside them. Takes recorded before the side was written down do not carry it.

print.title: The print of the main mix.
print.armed: MAIN is armed like any other strip, so the take already holds the mix you made on the night — the print. Exporting it writes that one capture out as a 24-bit WAV, beside the stems and never over them; the stems stay as they are.
print.notSummed: Nothing is summed to produce it. An offline sum of the stems would answer a different question: the stems are captured before the processing, so their sum is the console's inputs rather than the show. The print is the show.
print.clipping: Clipping is reported rather than hidden. A sample past the rail is held at it and counted, and the count and the true peak — measured before the rail — go on the take, so you learn the show clipped from the export rather than from someone listening to it later.
print.render: This is not the same action as a render. A render is the offline improvement pass over the tracks you select and writes a better copy of each of them; the export reads one file and writes one. That is also why a soundcheck playing does not block an export while it does block a render — refusing you your print because something is playing would be a rule with no cost behind it.
print.refuses: An export refuses rather than producing a file that is not the print: when the take carries no MAIN capture, when that capture holds no frames, when it cannot be read as an audio file, when there is not enough disk for it, and when one is already running. Each refusal says which of those it is.

empty.title: Tracks the take could not fill.
empty.header: A channel that was armed but never carried a buffer records a file with a header and nothing in it. The take is not refused for it and the track is not quietly dropped: the take counts how many of its tracks are known empty, and separately how many it cannot speak for at all, because a take made before the console measured this carries no answer rather than a zero.
empty.drops: An empty track is not the same thing as a take that lost frames. A channel with no signal path attached is skipped by the audio thread entirely, so nothing was dropped and the take honestly reports no drops. Two facts, and neither implies the other.
empty.soundcheck: The consequence you will meet is at soundcheck: a channel whose track in the take is empty is left on its live input rather than switched to silence, and the console names which channels those were. If that leaves nothing at all engaged, play refuses rather than running a transport no channel is listening to.
empty.tags: Both counts are on the take where you choose it. A take with known-empty tracks is tagged in record red with how many — 2 EMPTY — because that is the one that costs you a soundcheck, and a take whose tracks were never measured carries a dashed UNMEASURED instead, in a neutral colour: it is a take written before the console measured this, and painting it red would make every old take look broken. Dropped frames are a third tag again, and none of the three implies another.
empty.honest: Hiding an empty track would be worse than carrying an honest one. It is how you find out about a channel that recorded nothing from the library, rather than from a silent strip at the next soundcheck.

vsc.title: Running a virtual soundcheck.
vsc.intro: A virtual soundcheck plays a take back through the live desk as if the band were on stage again, so you can set up monitors, check a new plugin chain or train an operator without anyone playing a note. It is four steps, in order.
vsc.load: Load. Pick a take from the library. Nothing changes on the desk yet.
vsc.engage: Engage. This is the step that actually reaches the channels: every channel with a matching track in the take switches from listening to its live input to listening to that track instead. A channel the take has nothing for is left alone, still on its live input — a soundcheck never replaces a working microphone with silence.
vsc.play: Play. Moves the take's transport. Play means hear it, so pressing it with nothing engaged is refused rather than obeyed — nothing is listening to the take, so it would play unheard — engage a channel first, or check the take can serve these channels. A transport that ran to an empty room while the position number climbed is the kind of working control that wastes a soundcheck.
vsc.eject: Eject. One action: stops playback, hands every engaged channel back to its live input, and clears the loaded take. There is no partial eject.
vsc.rate: The live playback path still has no resampler and never will — a track handed to the graph has to already be at the graph's rate. But a take recorded at another rate is not refused for it: loading the take converts the tracks it will replay, offline, on disk, before a transport exists, and the node then opens ordinary files at its own rate. The conversion is cached in the take's own folder, so a second load costs one file check. Only what conversion cannot fix still refuses — no converter built in, or a conversion that could not finish — and that refusal names both rates.
vsc.exclusive: Recording and virtual soundcheck cannot run at the same time — both use the one audio graph, and starting one while the other holds it refuses rather than queueing silently behind it.

arriving.title: What this chapter does not describe yet, because it is not built.

items.wall: A wall-mode for arming — tap every channel tile to arm or disarm it, with select-all/none, the same gesture sends-on-fader already uses. Today, arming is one channel at a time.
items.transport: A play/pause toggle and a ±1 second nudge on the virtual-soundcheck transport, next to the scrub. Today, play is on or off and the position is set directly.
items.topBar: A top-bar record button and a recording LED visible from any page. Today, the record control lives on the channel strip.
items.metadata: The take’s files carrying BWF and iXML metadata (channel name, patch source, tap) so a DAW shows names without anyone retyping them. Today, that information lives only in the take’s own sidecar.
items.flac: A FLAC print. The export writes 24-bit WAV, which is the right depth and the wrong container for a deliverable that has to travel.
items.button: A button that fires the print. The export is served and it works; no surface offers it yet, so today it is fired over the API.
items.tapPicker: A tap picker on the channel. Which taps a channel records is a field the console serves and answers on, but no control writes it, so today a channel records its default set unless something drives it over the API.
