seo.title: Channel templates — OpenMixer
seo.description: Saving a channel’s processing for reuse, the factory instrument templates that state only the chain, and the preview that names every field an apply would move before it moves it.

hero.title: A known-good channel, carried from one gig to the next.
hero.lede: A channel config is one channel’s processing, saved under a name and applied to any other channel. The console ships a set of factory instrument templates alongside the ones you save, and both go on through the same door — but they say different things, and the difference is the whole chapter. Before any apply lands, the desk shows you exactly which fields it would move.

saving.title: Saving one.
saving.p1: In the library, pick the channel to capture, give it a name, and save. You can file it under a family — Vocals, Drums, Guitars — which groups it beside the factory templates for the same family in the picker. Naming no family is a choice rather than a missing field: it lands as an ungrouped entry.
saving.p2: The library is sorted by name, never by date. A config library is something you browse for the chain you want, not something you replay in the order you made it.
saving.notCaptures: And what it deliberately does not:

carried.dynamics: The EQ, the gate and the compressor.
carried.inserts: The insert rack and the order the processing runs in.
carried.polarity: Polarity, and the alignment delay with what it is aligned against.

notCarried.fader: The fader, the mute, the solo and solo-safe.
notCarried.identity: The channel’s name, its colour and its instrument.
notCarried.safe: Recall safe, and whether the channel is armed to record.
notCarried.patch: What is patched into the channel, and what the channel is linked to.

saving.p3: A config says what this channel’s processing is. It says nothing about where the channel is patched, how loud it sits in the mix, or what it is called — those belong to the show, and they are what a session saves.

factory.title: A factory template states the chain, and only the chain.
factory.p1: The instrument templates that come with the console — Kick In, Lead Vocal, and the rest — are a statement about the instrument: the EQ, the gate, the compressor, the insert rack and the order they run in. Applying one leaves the strip’s own facts exactly where you put them. Your gain, trim, pan, polarity and alignment do not move.
factory.p2: A kick drum’s compressor is much the same in every room. Its trim never is. Those two sentences are why the split exists: a template describes an instrument, and the head stage describes this strip and the source plugged into it.
factory.p3: A config you saved yourself is the other kind of statement — a whole one. It was captured from a real channel with a real head stage, so applying it moves the head stage too, including back to fresh if that is where you captured it. That is not an inconsistency between the two: a factory template never mentions the head stage, and something that is not mentioned is not changed.
factory.p4: Factory templates are read-only. They cannot be deleted, and a save cannot take one of their names out from under them.

preview.title: The preview of moves.
preview.p1: Applying a config is not additive, so before it lands the console asks the desk what would actually change and shows you the answer:

dialog.title: Apply “FOH Vocal Capture”?
dialog.note: A config is a whole statement about a channel, so applying it will move what CH3 holds now:

preview.p2: The list is one line per field that would move, computed by the console against what the channel holds at that moment — never by the surface, so what you are shown and what the door will do cannot disagree. A fact that rides several fields is listed field by field: you are warned about the 48 V, not about “the head amp”.
preview.p3: Three things read differently on purpose. A structured fact — an EQ curve, a gate, an insert rack — says replaced rather than printing a before and an after, because “from 8 bands to 8 bands” is not a readable sentence. A dash means the desk does not know what is there now, which happens on a head-amp fact from a preamp that has never reported; unknown is not zero. And a config applied to a channel that already matches it moves nothing, so it applies on one tap with no dialog at all — applying the same config twice must not ask twice.
preview.p4: The warning can be turned off with Don’t warn me again, which is a console-wide setting of its own. It is deliberately not the same switch as the one that arms destructive actions: an apply removes nothing, and an operator who turned off delete-arming did not ask to lose this.
preview.p5: Every way into an apply obeys it — the instrument picker on the processing view and the Apply button in the library both ask the same question. Cancelling leaves both doors shut, so a channel is never labelled with a template it did not get.
preview.p6: The question is asked by the console, not by the screen you happen to be using. An apply that would move something is refused at the door and comes back carrying the same list of moves, and nothing is written until the apply is sent again saying, in so many words, go ahead. That is why the dialog you see is not a screen the browser invented: the button fires, the console refuses, and the refusal is what the dialog is drawn from.
preview.p7: An OSC surface and an MCP client meet exactly the same refusal, with the same list, and answer it the same way. There is no client that quietly applies without asking, and no client that has to be taught the rule: the desk holds it, in one place, and every surface renders what the desk said.
preview.p8: Both the sign-off setting and the list of moves are read afresh on every attempt. Turning the warning off takes effect on the next apply rather than on the next reload, and a console that cannot read its own setting asks rather than assumes.

history.title: An apply clears the history.
history.text: Applying a config restates a whole channel in one action, so it empties the journal rather than appearing in it — the same rule that covers loading a session or recalling a scene. Saving or deleting a config empties it too. See {link} for what that means and what the way back is.

rest.text: The library is {library}, the apply is {apply} and the preview is the read-only sibling at {preview}, whose state is what a refused apply hands back. The console lists every row that asks before it fires in its own index, so a client knows to expect the question rather than guessing — both rows are in the {link}.

seo.title: Zynthian: plugin-hostd as its plugin host | OpenMixer
seo.description: Zynthian running its LV2 and CLAP plugins under plugin-hostd: what it is, what it changes, how to install and use it, the measured figures and where it stands.

hero.title: Zynthian: plugin-hostd as its plugin host.
hero.lede: How to install it, how to use it, what it changes in Zynthian and where it stands. The method and every table are in the technical notes linked at the end.

what.title: What it is.
what.p1: Zynthian is an open synthesizer and effects platform on a Raspberry Pi. It runs LV2 plugins through its own engines: mod-host, behind MOD-UI, which runs its effect chains, and jalv, which runs one plugin per process. plugin-hostd speaks mod-host's protocol and runs each plugin, LV2 or CLAP, in a worker process, so a plugin that crashes takes down only its own worker, which is put back with its settings. A whole chain can run in one worker instead of one process per plugin, and plugin-qualify measures each plugin on the device first, so the menus are built from what it found.
what.p2: With it Zynthian gets a plugin-hostd engine beside jalv for LV2 and CLAP plugins in chains, plugin-hostd as a switchable replacement for mod-host under MOD-UI, plugin menus ordered and tagged from per-plugin qualification records, and chains whose plugins the daemon groups into as few workers as their pins allow.

changes.title: How much it changes in Zynthian.
changes.p1: Nothing in Zynthian depends on it. It stays on jackd: no file that configures JACK changes, and no PipeWire is involved. As offered to Zynthian, the plugin-hostd engine stays off until a user turns it on, and MOD-UI keeps mod-host until a user switches its backend; going back is the same setting.
changes.p2: FreeMixer's forks of zynthian-ui and zynthian-sys have it on: plugin-hostd is the default plugin engine, in place of jalv, and MOD-UI's default backend, in place of mod-host, and the qualification sync is enabled. Every LV2 and CLAP plugin is listed once, under plugin-hostd and marked (PH). A plugin our host refuses stays in the list, marked not working, with its reason; nothing moves it to jalv. jalv remains an engine you can select.
changes.p3: What runs when nobody uses it: the interface starts a daemon only when a chain holds a plugin-hostd plugin. What stays enabled is the qualification sync, two minutes after boot at the lowest CPU and disk priority, skipping every plugin whose files have not changed, and omx-panel's MOD GUI and complement syncs. All of them can be disabled; the first sync on a device with many plugins is long.

image.title: The image
image.where: ZynthianOS Vangelis for the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, with the forks of zynthian-ui and zynthian-sys, the OpenMixer apt repository, and plugin-hostd, omx-clap-host, omx-plugins, omx-panel and plugin-qualify installed and made the default. It is built from upstream's released Vangelis image with the fork's own update steps, as the fork's docs/openmixer-image.md describes, and will be a release of FreeMixer's zynthian-sys fork, in parts with their sums. It is not published yet: until it is, install the packages on a Vangelis you already run, as below.
image.firstBoot: The first boot does what any Zynthian card does once: it detects the kit, regenerates the SSH keys and the web certificate, creates the Wi-Fi access point, grows the file system to the card, and reboots once. Two minutes after boot the qualification sync starts in the background, at the lowest priority, and does not hold the boot; with the qualification records package installed it only checks that the plugin files are the ones the records describe.

existing.title: On an existing Vangelis
existing.p1: A Vangelis system already running needs no new image. As root, add the OpenMixer repository and install the packages:
existing.p2: openmixer-release carries the signing key and the apt source of the running Debian release. This enables no service: mod-host, MOD-UI, jalv and the menus stay as they were until you switch them.

switch.title: Turn it on, and back off
switch.p1: Three settings, each undone by setting it back:

use.title: Use it.
use.intro: With the plugin-hostd engine on, a plugin's menu entry ends in "(PH)". Select a chain, open its options and use Add Audio-FX processor; the plugin's controller pages follow its own sections.

group.title: A group: plugins in series in one worker
group.p1: With grouping on, a run of plugins in series in a chain shares one worker process and one JACK client instead of one process each. A group is what the chain has in series with nothing between: a parallel slot, the mixer strip or a jalv plugin ends it. A processor that runs alone has a Grouping entry in its options saying why.
group.p2: Grouping is off unless you set it. It saves most of the memory of one process per plugin: 24 plugins in one chain take about 64 MB, against about 110 MB under mod-host.

strip.title: A channel strip as plugins
strip.p1: EQ and dynamics per chain are ordinary effects in that chain; Zynthian's mixer keeps its level, pan and sends. Either add separate plugins (omx keyed-gate, omx eq8, omx comp: you choose each one and its order, and eq8 has eight bands), or one plugin, omx strip: input trim, filters, a gate, four EQ bands and a compressor in stereo, in one load and one worker, its five stages in any order.

mixbus.title: Shared effects on a Mixbus
mixbus.p1: One effect on a bus instead of one per chain, fed from each chain with Zynthian's own sends:
mixbus.step1: Add a chain and choose Mixbus. In its options, Add Audio-FX processor: omx reverb, then omx delay, each "(PH)".
mixbus.step2: In each chain that should feed it, open the mixer processor's controller page and raise the send level for that Mixbus, pre or post fader.
mixbus.p2: A plugin-hostd plugin behaves in a Mixbus as in any chain. A slot holds one processor or several, and several are parallel; a worker runs its plugins in series in one JACK client, so with grouping on:

series.runs: A and B in one worker, one JACK client

parallel.runs: a worker each: B and C are parallel, three clients

mixed.runs: A with B, a worker each for C and D, E with F: four clients

strip.runs: a worker each: the strip is in the signal's way

jalv.runs: a worker each, and the jalv plugin's own client

mixbus.p3: Send levels, pre and post fader, and pinning or moving a Mixbus are Zynthian's mixer and chain manager: none of them sends anything to the daemon. Measured at JACK ports, series, parallel and Mixbus chains give the levels they should: unity in series, +6.02 dB for two in parallel, the strip's -20 dB where it sits.

why.title: Why
why.p1: A Pi 5 has four cores. A synth plays many voices at once, and every block of audio has a deadline: all the voices must be computed before it is due. Run one after another, they all use one core. That core sets how many notes you can play, however idle the other three are.
why.p2: Some synths split their voices into tasks and ask the host to run them (CLAP's thread-pool extension). Tasks like that can run side by side, if the host lets them.

how.title: How it works
how.p1: omx-clap-host starts helper threads: one for each core the plugin's worker may use, minus one, because the audio thread takes the last core. Each helper is pinned to its core, runs at the audio thread's real-time priority and sleeps between blocks.
how.p2: When the plugin asks for its tasks, the helpers and the audio thread take them one by one, and the call returns when the last is done. If the priority cannot be set, there are no helpers and the tasks run as before, in turn.

gate.title: Who gets helpers
gate.p1: Not every plugin. Helper threads are given plugin by plugin, never everywhere. A plugin gets them only if its qualification found it real-time safe, with the helpers watched too, and faster with them. A task that allocates or waits on a lock would make every core miss the deadline.
gate.p2: Any other plugin runs as before: its tasks one after another on the audio thread. A plugin that gets helpers runs in a worker of its own, which plugin-hostd starts with the pool on.

switch.title: How to switch it
switch.p1: It is an option of omx-clap-host:
switch.qualified: qualified (the default): only plugins whose qualification grants it get helpers. plugin-hostd gives each worker the right setting, so on Zynthian you do not set it.
switch.on: on: every plugin that uses the extension gets helpers.
switch.off: off: every plugin runs its tasks in turn.

measured.title: What it gives
measured.p1: Measured on a Raspberry Pi 5 at 48 kHz and 256 frames, so the block is due in 5333 µs. The plugin is a test plugin that splits each block into 16 tasks, because no plugin on the Pi asks for tasks yet, Surge XT included. The time is the mean cost of one block, with the helpers off and on:
measured.p2: At 512 frames, the 48-voice load takes 6.6 ms of the 10.7 ms block with the helpers off and 1.7 ms with them on. No block went over its deadline in any run.
measured.p3: This is the best case: equal tasks that share nothing. A real instrument has not been measured with it, so there is no Surge XT figure. Surge XT does not split its voices, and for it the cores come from running each instrument in a worker of its own: four instances with 16 notes each ran at 14 to 15 % of a core each.

seo.title: FAQ — OpenMixer
seo.description: Straight answers about what OpenMixer is, what it needs, what it can carry today, and what it cannot.

hero.title: Questions with straight answers.
hero.lede: Including the ones where the answer is no.

remote.q: Is this a remote control for a mixing desk?
a: No. Most software that looks like a mixer is a surface for a hardware console somewhere else. OpenMixer is the console: the audio runs through it. Inputs arrive from a stagebox or any PipeWire source, each channel has a fader and a processing chain, the buses are summed in the console’s own signal processing, and the mix goes back out to the PA.
There is no hardware desk in the signal path. Real consoles can be attached as controllers, but that is an optional side path.

multiUser.q: Can several people mix at the same time?
a: Yes, and that is the design rather than a feature bolted on. One server holds the whole mix and every screen is a view of it, so a fader moved on the laptop at front of house moves on the tablet on the wing at the same time.
Every client is a remote client, including the one running on the same machine. There is no privileged surface.

offline.q: Does it need an internet connection?
a: No, and it is built on the assumption that it will not have one. The surface, the plugin catalog and the entire documentation set are served from the machine itself. Nothing is fetched from the network to draw a page.
GPL-3.0-or-later, and every package in the workspace carries the same licence.

monoFold.q: Why does the mono fold have no level control?
a: Because there is only one correct number, and it is not a matter of taste. A stereo pair carrying centred mono content is the same signal on both legs, and summing two identical legs to one socket makes the result twice as loud in amplitude — six decibels hotter — than either leg on its own.

The fold applies a fixed −6 dB to undo exactly that doubling, so a centred mix lands at the same level folded as it was in stereo. A dial there would only let someone turn the correct answer into a wrong one.
monoFold.link: Why the mono fold and the pan law are fixed numbers, not settings

twiceLoud.q: How many dB is twice as loud?
a: It depends what is doubling. Two identical signals summed together double in amplitude, which is +6 dB. Two unrelated signals summed together double in power, which is +3 dB. Perceived loudness — what a listener actually hears — is a slower, more approximate curve: it takes roughly +10 dB before most people agree something sounds twice as loud.
All three are real and none of them is wrong; they answer different questions.

powerAmplitude.q: What is the difference between power, amplitude and loudness?
a: Amplitude is the size of the waveform itself — the voltage, the sample value — and it is what a fader multiplies. Power is proportional to amplitude squared, and it is what a meter of energy reads. Loudness is what a listener perceives, and it grows more slowly than either.
The decibel is the common ratio between all three: 20·log10 of a ratio for amplitude, 10·log10 for power, so a doubling of amplitude and a quadrupling of power both read as the same six decibels.

package.q: Is there a package I can install?
a: For the plugin hosts, yes: omx-clap-host and plugin-hostd are signed packages for Fedora and for Debian, Raspberry Pi OS and Zynthian, on x86_64 and ARM64.
The console itself is not published yet.

quietChannel.q: A channel has gone quiet and its mute button is not lit — what is holding it?
a: Most likely solo in place. When the cue mode is SIP and something is soloed, every channel that is neither soloed nor solo-safe is silenced — that is what solo in place means, and it is the mode that silences the house rather than only the headphones.

The channel says so rather than leaving you to work it out: the mute state carries a separate flag for it, and the strip gets its own badge and dims like anything else that is not being heard — without the mute button pretending somebody pressed it. The way back is to clear the solo, or to make the strip solo-safe.
The other two holds read the same way: a mute group holding the channel, and a panic. Each is its own flag, owned by whatever set it.

requirements.q: What does it need to run?
a: Linux with PipeWire, Node 22 or newer, and pnpm to build. Audio comes from anything PipeWire can see, which includes a plain USB interface, so a stagebox is not required to try it.
The reference rig is a Roland REAC stagebox with an RME Babyface Pro as the clock master, on Fedora.

pllClock.q: Why does the rig need a PLL clock?
a: Because OpenMixer’s own timing comes from whatever hardware drives the audio graph, and it hands that timing to every stagebox as the REAC master. A professional interface with a phase-locked loop, the RME on the reference rig, keeps a steady clock and filters jitter; a free-running crystal drifts and a software timer jitters with the machine.
The REAC clock panel shows each segment’s pace source: phc or graph-ref means the rig is locked, free-run means it is not.
48 kHz and 96 kHz have both been run on the rig, including a change between them with the console live.
44.1 kHz has been run on the rig too: an S-0808 re-paced to 44.1 kHz and back to 48, with a tone heard through it.

lv2.q: Do I need LV2 plugins to use it?
a: No. The faders, EQ, gate, compressor, delay, reverb, buses and routing are all native to the console and need nothing installed.

A fresh machine has no LV2 plugins, so the plugin picker starts empty. That is expected, not a fault. Curated sets can be installed separately, tiered by measured round-trip latency so the live-safe choice is the default.

offlineMode.q: The surface shows a whole console but nothing happens when I move a fader.
a: That is the offline mode, and the connection indicator in the header says so. With no server reachable, the surface falls back to a simulated board so the controls can be learned without a console behind them.

It is easy to miss precisely because it is not an error message. If you expected a live desk, the server is not reachable — check that it is running and that the surface is being served the endpoint you think it is.

script.q: Can I drive it from a script?
a: Yes. The whole console is a REST surface: every entity answers GET, PATCH and OPTIONS at a plain, typeable address, and curl is a first-class client rather than a debugging trick.

OPTIONS on any entity publishes its contract — the writable fields, the ranges, the units and the enumerated options — so a client can be written against what the server says rather than against a copy of the rules.

watch.q: How do I follow state without polling?
a: Add ?watch=1 to any GET and it becomes a server-sent event stream that emits exactly what that GET returns, starting with a full snapshot.

For a whole surface, watch the root: one stream carries every committed change on the console. Prefer that to opening a stream per panel — browsers allow only six connections to an origin, and spending them all makes every later request queue.
No, and there will not be one. There is one door and one wire.

storage.q: Where are recordings stored, and in what format?
a: Under the console’s state directory — {'$'}XDG_STATE_HOME/openmixer/takes/<id>/, or ~/.local/state/openmixer/takes/<id>/ if that variable is not set, or wherever --state-dir points. Each track is its own file: one mono 32-bit float channel, WAV while it stays under 4 GB and RF64 once it does not, at the sample rate the graph was running when the take was recorded.
RF64 only changes the header once a file needs 64-bit sizes; any DAW that opens a WAV opens either form the same way.

whatRecorded.q: What gets recorded when I press record?
a: Every patched input and MAIN, by default, with a per-channel opt-out — there is no channel list to fill in first. Aux and matrix channels are not armed unless you ask for them.

Each armed channel is captured at two points, simultaneously: its raw input, taken straight after the trim, and its post-fader signal. An input channel is offered a third point, pre-fader, and the points are a set rather than a choice — a channel can record pre and post fader at once. A bus master is offered post-fader only.
No control on the surface changes that set yet, so today a channel records its default unless something writes the field over the API.

armMidTake.q: Can I arm or unarm a channel while a take is running?
a: No. A take’s channel set is fixed the moment it starts. Changing an arm setting mid-take affects the next take, not the one in progress — otherwise nobody could say afterwards what the first ten minutes of a show actually held.

armMany.q: Is there a quick way to arm a lot of channels at once?
a: Not yet. Arming is one channel at a time today. A wall-mode — tap tiles across the whole fader wall to arm or disarm them, with select-all and select-none — is designed, using the same mechanism sends-on-fader already has, but it is not built.

print.q: Can I get one file of the show out, rather than the whole stem folder?
a: Yes — the print. MAIN is armed like every other strip, so the take already holds the mix you made on the night, and exporting writes that one capture out as a 24-bit WAV beside the stems. Nothing is summed to produce it: the stems are captured before the processing, so a sum of them would be the console’s inputs rather than the show.

Two limits worth knowing. It is WAV and not yet FLAC, which is the right depth in the wrong container for something that has to travel. And no button fires it yet — the export is served and works, but today it is fired over the API.

The stems themselves are never rewritten and there is no lossy stem export, because a mixer that recorded a show in a lesser format than it captured it would be throwing away the reason to have recorded at all.

emptyTrack.q: A track in my take is an empty file. Did the recording fail?
a: No, and the take says so rather than hiding it. A channel that was armed but had nothing patched into it is skipped by the audio thread entirely, so its file is a header with no frames — and no frames were dropped, which is why the take honestly reports no drops at the same time. Emptiness and dropped frames are two different facts.

The take counts how many of its tracks are known empty, and separately how many it cannot speak for at all, because a take made before the console measured this carries no answer rather than a zero. At soundcheck, a channel whose track is empty is left on its live input instead of being switched to silence, and the console names which ones those were.

Loading a recorded take back into the live desk so it plays as if the band were on stage again. Load a take, engage it, and every channel with a matching track switches from its live input to that track — so you can set monitors, try a plugin chain or train an operator without anyone in the room performing.
A channel the take has nothing for stays on its live input; a soundcheck never replaces a working microphone with silence.

playRefused.q: I pressed play and the desk refused it — why?
a: “nothing is listening to the take, so it would play unheard — engage a channel first, or check the take can serve these channels.” Play is a separate step from engage: engage is what switches channels from their live inputs over to the take’s tracks, and play only moves the transport.
Press engage first. If you did engage and still get this, the take has no track for any of the channels you engaged — check the take is the one you meant.
Play means hear it, which is why this refuses rather than obeying. A transport running to an empty room while the position number climbs is the kind of working control that wastes a soundcheck.

otherRate.q: Can I run a virtual soundcheck at a different sample rate than the take was recorded at?
a: Yes. The live playback path still has no resampler, deliberately, so loading a take at another rate converts the tracks it will replay, offline, on disk, before the transport exists — the graph only ever opens files already at its own rate. The conversion is cached in the take, so a second load costs one file check.
A mismatch only refuses when conversion cannot happen: no converter built in, or a conversion that could not finish. That refusal still names both rates.

recordAndPlay.q: Can I record and run a virtual soundcheck at the same time?
a: No. Recording and playback both use the one audio graph, and starting either while the other holds it refuses outright rather than queueing silently behind it.

trust.q: Can I trust recording and the virtual soundcheck on a real show?
a: Recording works: every armed track is captured to disk, and a take plays back through the console.

insertBudget.q: “the destination cannot afford this insert chain”
a: The plugins on that rack add more delay than the place the signal is going can carry. The budget belongs to the destination, not to the plugin: a monitor destination is held to 5 ms and refuses; a program destination has 100 ms and an effects destination 60 ms, and those two let the edit through and warn instead.

The reason underneath names the plugin and the numbers — “ZaMaximX2 puts this chain at 7.4 ms — over the 5.0 ms budget for a monitor destination at 48000 Hz. On a monitor send the performer hears themself that late.”
Take out the plugin it names, replace it with a lower-latency one, or rack it somewhere the delay does not matter. Bypassing does not help: a bypassed plugin still costs its delay.

monoStrip.q: “… has 2 audio legs and this strip is mono — rack the plugin’s mono build, or make the strip stereo.”
a: You racked a stereo plugin on a mono strip. The sentence names both ways out because both are real: most plugin families ship a mono build of the same processor, and a strip fed a stereo source can be made stereo.

It refuses rather than folding the plugin down because folding would be silent and wrong. Both output legs land in the strip’s one input port and are summed there — a measured 6.02 dB lift on the main mix from a stereo EQ sitting at unity, doing nothing. The mono twin of the same plugin moves the mix by 0.00 dB.
Nothing is written when it fires, and the whole rack is refused rather than quietly trimmed. Only the first plugin that does not fit is named.

You will meet it less often than you used to: the strip’s own rack door publishes what fits that strip, so the picker greys a plugin too wide for it instead of offering it. The refusal is still there for everything that does not go through the picker, and for a strip that changes width under a rack it already holds.

postFader.q: “a plugin cannot run at Post-Fader yet — rack it at one of Top-Of-Ch, Post-Trim, Pre-EQ, Post-EQ, Pre-Fader instead”
a: Post-Fader is a named point on the channel chain that does not carry audio yet. The slot is deliberately still there rather than tidied away, because a missing mechanism you can see is better than one that has quietly vanished.

Rack the plugin at one of the five points the sentence lists, or put it in the strip’s insert rack, which is after the fader anyway. When Post-Fader carries audio it joins the list and this stops firing, with no change needed to anything that talks to the console.

hostSlots.q: “the plugin host has no instance slot left … restart the plugin host to reclaim them”
a: The sentence carries two numbers — how many slots the host has in all, and how many are held by plugins that were un-racked and never freed. When the second number is close to the first, that is the whole diagnosis: the host leaks a slot per un-rack, so a long session of trying plugins runs it dry.
Restart the plugin host. Nothing about the console’s own processing depends on it, so the desk keeps mixing while it comes back.

takeRate.q: “the take was recorded at 48000 Hz and the desk is running at 96000 Hz — match the clock or record it again”
a: A mismatched take is usually converted for you: loading it resamples the tracks it will replay, offline, before you press engage, so play runs at the graph’s own rate. This refusal is what is left over — no converter built into this install, or a conversion that could not finish — and it still means the take cannot play here as it stands.
Set the graph to the take’s rate, or record a new take at the rate you are running.

soundcheckLoaded.q: “a virtual soundcheck is loaded — eject it before recording, so the take on the disk is the room and not the recording”
a: A soundcheck is feeding the channels from a take, so recording now would capture that take back to disk rather than the room. Eject, then record.
It goes the other way too: “a take is being recorded — stop it before playing one back.” Both directions use the one audio graph and refuse rather than queueing silently behind each other.

noChannel.q: “no channel would be recorded: check that inputs are patched and that they have not been taken out of the take”
a: Nothing is armed. Because arming is opt-out rather than opt-in, this almost always means nothing is patched — a channel with no source records nothing worth keeping and is left out of the derivation until something is patched into it.
Patch an input, or put back a channel you took out of the take. It refuses before the first sample rather than leaving you with a folder to clean up.

diskSpace.q: “the disk holds 3221225472 bytes and this take needs at least 15032385536 before it will start”
a: The recorder works out what the take needs to open safely and checks it first. The numbers are both there on purpose: “not enough space” is not something you can act on, and “it needs 14 GB and there is 3” is.
Free space or point the state directory somewhere with room. The same check guards a render and the print export, each with its own numbers.

noMain.q: “this take carries no MAIN capture, and the print is the main capture”
a: The print is not a mixdown the console computes; it is the MAIN capture the take already holds. A take recorded with MAIN taken out of it has nothing to print.
Nothing can be done for that take. Leave MAIN armed — it is armed by default — and the next take will have one.

applyConfirm.q: “applying this would move 5 of what the channel holds (gain, trim, pan, eq, inserts) — confirm to go ahead”
a: A channel config is a whole statement about a channel, so applying one to a channel that already holds something moves what is there. The console works out exactly which fields would move, refuses the apply, and hands the list back with the refusal — nothing is written.

Send it again saying confirm, and it applies. The list is the same list the dialog shows you, because the dialog is drawn from this refusal rather than from a preview the surface fetched for itself; a browser, an OSC surface and an MCP client all meet it and answer it the same way.

An apply that would move nothing is never held — applying the same config twice does not ask twice. And if you would rather not be asked at all, the sign-off is a console setting of its own, read afresh on every attempt. It is deliberately not the switch that arms destructive actions: an apply removes nothing.

undoMoved.q: “db reads −3.0 now, not the −12.0 this step left (changed by entry 41)”
a: The change you asked to take back has moved since — by another operator, by a control surface, or by a later gesture of your own. Writing the old value now would jump the fader from a value nobody expects to one nobody asked for.

Ctrl+Z gets the same sentence as the Undo this button in the list, and so does redo: the console compares the step against what the field reads now before it replays anything, and asks one question at all three doors rather than being careful in the list and blunt at the top of it. Nothing is written while the question stands.

The console asks instead of choosing: go back anyway, or leave it. A jump-back taken from a row in the list records in its new entry that it went over the later one, so the list says a jump-back happened. It never retries behind your back, and if the desk moves again while the question is on screen the offer is dropped rather than answered against a stale value.

mastering.q: “You asked to be the mixer, but a desk is already mastering this segment.”
a: One master per REAC segment is the protocol’s law, not a policy of this console’s. Another desk holds the wire, so the console is holding and has asserted nothing on it.

The panel offers the one gesture that resolves it: switch the segment to recorder and join the wire as the box end. Or take the other desk off the segment, at which point automatic picks it up on its own.

Two related sentences have no button, because the remedy is not the console’s to make. “A stagebox on this segment has its REAC Mode switch on M (master)” means walking to the box, setting the switch to S and power-cycling it. “Something is mastering this segment and the console cannot tell what it is” means finding out what else is on that wire.

slaveRate.q: “A slave segment has no rate to set — it follows the foreign master’s pace”
a: The segment is following another desk, and a follower has no pace of its own to set — it locks to the master’s, physically.

If the rate is yours to choose, take the segment first: promote it to mixer, then set the rate on it. That is two confirmations rather than one, and each of them re-establishes the segment on the wire.

realShow.q: Can I mix a real show on this?
a: It mixes real shows on a real rig, so the honest answer is that it depends on what your show needs.

Channels, buses, sends, DCAs, mute groups, the matrix, EQ, dynamics, the analyser, feedback correction, delay alignment, plugin inserts, recording and REAC stageboxes have all been driven and measured. Of the control surfaces, only the X-Touch has been tested on hardware. Read the known limitations before you commit to it, not afterwards.

reachAudio.q: How do you know a control actually reaches the audio?
a: By measuring audio. A control can read back perfectly and reach nothing at all, and a test that only asks the model whether it changed will agree with that forever.

So the signal processing is checked against values worked out on paper rather than captured from a run, graph changes are verified against the live graph rather than a model of it, and a phantom power claim needs a person at the connector rather than an indicator on a screen.
S-series boxes over REAC, including head-amp control — phantom, pad and sensitivity — which is what makes a box a stagebox rather than a stream. Two boxes have been established at once on the rig.
The REAC transport itself is a separate project, FreeREAC, and its own site covers what is known about the protocol and which boxes have been worked with.

seo.title: Features — OpenMixer
seo.description: What the console does today, each item labelled by how far it has actually been proven: driven on the rig, measured in audio, or still landing.

hero.title: What it does, and how far it has been proven.
hero.lede: Three labels, and they mean different things. Proven on the rig means a person drove it on a real console with real hardware. Built and measured means audio was measured through it. In development means the code is landing and nothing has proved it yet.

desk.title: The desk
desk.p1: Input channels with head gain, trim, pan, polarity, phantom and pad; a full processing rack per strip; buses, aux sends with pre and post tap points, DCAs, a matrix, mix-minus, stereo channel linking and output inserts.
desk.p2: Sessions persist and reload at boot. Scenes recall. Mute groups, solo (PFL, AFL, solo-in-place with an arming step), a dim, and two panic buttons that separate the mains from the whole console.
desk.p3: Mix-minus is a first-class kind with its own addresses rather than an index-offset hack. Buses and MAIN are strips like any other — there are no master-only mechanisms hiding behind a different code path.
desk.p4: A show load is a clean slate: loading show B over show A returns every channel and every setting B does not mention to what a freshly built strip carries. The one exception is the head-amp, because a show file never asserts phantom, pad or gain onto a real preamp.

native.title: Native processing
native.p1: A parametric EQ bank with a graphical curve, a gate, a compressor, a delay line and a reverb — all of them in the console's own C node, all of them checked against hand-computed values rather than against a recording of themselves.
native.p2: Moving a fader, a mute, a pan, an EQ band, a gate, a compressor, a delay or a reverb moves audio on the kinds where the console says it does, and where it cannot, it refuses by name rather than lying. That is the strongest part of the console and it is worth saying plainly.

rta.title: Real-time analyser
rta.p1: A native FFT with a multi-resolution zoom tier — bins of about 0.73 Hz below a 300 Hz crossover, where a broad-band analyser tells you nothing useful. Peak hold, pre- and post-EQ overlay, and a per-band difference trace.
rta.p2: Nothing computes unwatched. The analyser is demand-gated per channel and the arming survives a reload because it rides the session, not the browser. Buses have their own analyser, proven by feeding a tone into one bus and reading the spectrum peak at the fed frequency while a bus with no send read a floor with no peak.
rta.shotAlt: The analyser at full height: a live spectrum from 20 Hz to 20 kHz with peak hold and four EQ band handles on the curve.
rta.shotCaption: The analyser running on a live input, with the channel's EQ band handles on the same curve.

feedback.title: Feedback detection and correction
feedback.p1: The detector watches for the signature of a ringing room and the corrector plants notches into the channel EQ. Two modes with genuinely different behaviour: a ring-out pass plants a true full-cut notch at a very high Q, while live mode plants a gain-carrying bell whose depth comes from the signal's peak-to-average ratio.
feedback.p2: Live-mode notches lift again in staged ramps as the room settles — two thirds, one third, gone — and re-clamp with a doubled hold if the frequency comes back. It never touches an operator's own bands; only its own tagged ones.
feedback.p3: It is offered on inputs and on every bus strip, aux, mix, matrix and MAIN alike: a single detector on MAIN, planting its notches in MAIN's own EQ, is a sanctioned way to work.

align.title: Smart alignment
align.p1: Two microphones on one source arrive at different times. Pick the reference, watch coherence rise, apply. The fit reads the phase slope across frequency, which is why it needs programme material — a pure tone cannot measure delay, because a sine occupies one bin.
align.p2: It corrects with delay and polarity, and reports the residual rather than silently correcting it. A control that says "137°" without naming the frequency invites the operator to discover that changing the analysis band changes the answer.
align.p3: A saved show carries the alignment, and loading the show restores it. Loading a show that never had an alignment clears it.
align.converge: Repeated apply converges: 4.748 → 0.252 → 0.016 → 0.001 → 0.000 ms, at a coherence of 1.000.

lv2.title: LV2 plugin inserts
lv2.p1: Per-strip and per-output insert chains for LV2 and CLAP plugins, with a plugin picker and an editor generated from the plugin's own ports.
lv2.p2: The catalog tiers a plugin by measured round-trip latency — live at 5 ms or under, studio above it, ambiguous ones quarantined — and then ranks within a tier by curation and CPU cost, so the live-safe choice wins by default.
lv2.p3: Insert audio is verified by measurement rather than by inspection: a tone through a real graph, a notch racked as an LV2, and a reading at the other end. The reference measurement is a baseline of −12.04 dBFS, the same notch through the plugin door at −100.56 dBFS, and bypass returning to −12.04 exactly — 88.52 dB of cut, through the plugin and not around it.
lv2.p4: Plugin delay compensation is applied: the channels that feed one bus are delayed to match the feed with the most insert latency, and on the rig a strip with an out-of-process insert racked measures 0 samples of lag against its pair.

reac.title: REAC stageboxes
reac.p1: Roland S-series stageboxes are discovered, patched and driven — including head-amp control, which is what makes them a stagebox rather than a stream. Two boxes have been established at once on the rig with all 128 links intact across a rebind, and a live 48 to 96 kHz re-pace has been run with the house up.
reac.p2: Phantom power has been confirmed physically at the XLR pins on two inputs with the console independently agreeing. Three sources, one answer — which is the only kind of confirmation a phantom claim is allowed to have.
reac.p3: The transport lives in the sibling FreeREAC projects, not in this project. OpenMixer holds the control path: discovery, head-amp, the patch and the adapter side.
reac.p4: 44.1 kHz works as well: a stagebox re-paces to 44.1 kHz and back to 48 kHz with the signal passing through it.
reac.shotAlt: The patchbay: a crosspoint grid of sources against channels, with detected stageboxes grouped down the left edge.
reac.shotCaption: The patchbay. Sources down the side, channels across the top, detected stageboxes grouped and counted.

surface.title: The web surface
surface.p1: A fader wall with banks and user pages, channel strips with a reorderable processing rack, bus-send and matrix views, the patchbay, a graph view, a telemetry view, and a docked multi-window workspace that can be pulled apart and saved as a layout.
surface.p2: The banks roll under the mouse wheel, anywhere over the rail that is not itself a control: one notch is one bank, the same wrapping step the ◀ ▶ buttons make, and a trackpad swipe moves one bank rather than a dozen. A wheel over a fader still trims that fader.
surface.p3: English, Catalan and Spanish. Dark, light and a high-contrast theme, on an axis independent of the console personality.
surface.p4: Its entire state intake is one EventSource and nothing else. The surface cannot open a second channel to the console, by construction rather than by convention.
surface.p5: A change is a PATCH, never a reconnect. There is a deploy gate that drives a real browser through real gestures against a real console and measures long tasks, request bursts, stream re-dials, framework warnings and server-side heals — a green unit suite cannot see a frozen tab.

surfaces.title: Control surfaces
surfaces.p1: The Behringer X-Touch and X-Touch Mini are implemented as a bidirectional client: surface gestures become canonical operations, and canonical state drives the motor faders, the LEDs, the V-Pot rings, the scribble strips and the meters. It is wired into the production composition root.
surfaces.p2: The X-Touch has been run on a real surface: the faders and motors, mute, solo, the V-Pots, SELECT, the master fader, the scribble strips, the meter ladder, a power-cycle and a console restart. The bugs that run found are fixed. The X-Touch Mini and the adapters for Midas, X32/M32 and Roland have not been run on a real surface.

control24.text: The Digidesign Control{'|'}24 and ProControl talk DigiNet over Ethernet. Their protocol library, libdiginet, is released; the console does not drive one. {link}

recorder.title: Recorder and virtual soundcard
recorder.p1: Multitrack capture to RF64 takes at 48 kHz, a take library, and a virtual soundcard so another application on the same machine can be a source or a destination on the desk.
recorder.p2: The code is in: the C capture and playback paths, the RF64 writer and its oracle tests, and the server rows. The arm set is derived rather than stored. The live playback path has no resampler, so a take recorded at another rate is converted offline, on disk, before playback starts.
recorder.p3: Recording works: a real take on the rig wrote eighty-four tracks, and a round-trip test records a take and plays it back through the audio graph.

limits.title: Known limitations.
limits.intro: A product page that lists only what works is not a description of a console. These are the limits worth knowing before OpenMixer carries anything you cannot afford to lose.
limits.surfacesHead: Only the X-Touch has been tested on hardware.
limits.surfacesBody: The X-Touch Mini and the adapters for Midas, X32/M32 and Roland have not been run on a real surface.
limits.packageHead: The console is not packaged yet.
limits.footer: This list changes as work lands. The documentation set carries the current version of it.

hosting.title: The plugin host.
hosting.intro: The host that runs the plugins serves the console and Zynthian alike. Each card says where a feature stands on the console, on Zynthian and on any other host. "To confirm" means this state has not been checked on the console yet.

seo.title: Get it — OpenMixer
seo.description: Install the OpenMixer plugin hosts from signed packages for Fedora, Debian, Raspberry Pi OS and Zynthian, and try them.

hero.title: Install from our packages.
hero.lede: omx-clap-host and plugin-hostd, the plugin hosts OpenMixer runs on, are signed packages for Fedora and Debian, on x86_64 and ARM64. The console itself is not published yet.

install.title: Add the repository, install the packages.

gettingStarted.text: It takes a fresh install from silence to one channel audible in the main mix. Everything else in the manual assumes you have done it once.
gettingStarted.link: Read it before you open the surface.

seo.title: OpenMixer — a mixing console, built in software
seo.description: OpenMixer is a live mixer for Linux: its own real-time engine inside PipeWire, stagebox in, PA out, any browser as its surface, and every plugin without betting the show on it.

hero.title: A mixing console, built from scratch in software.
hero.lede: OpenMixer is a live mixer for Linux. Audio comes in from a stagebox, is mixed by OpenMixer's own real-time engine inside PipeWire, and goes back out to the PA. There is no hardware console in the signal path: the console is the software, and every browser on the network is its surface.
hero.wallLabel: An illustration of the OpenMixer fader wall: seven channel strips and the main bus, each with a gain knob, a level meter and a fader.

console.title: Not a remote for someone else's desk. The mixer itself.
console.lede: Most mixer apps are remote controls for a hardware console. With OpenMixer the audio runs through the software: one console model that fits no particular desk sits in the middle, and the engine, the surfaces and the I/O all plug into it. {link}.
console.shotAlt: The OpenMixer surface: a channel strip with gain, trim, pan, phantom and the EQ curve above a wall of sixteen faders and the main strip.
console.shotCaption: The running console. Channel 9 selected on its processing rack; sixteen input strips and MAIN below.

in.title: Stagebox
in.what: Native REAC, or any PipeWire device

strip.title: The channel strip
strip.what: Head gain, EQ, gate, compressor, pan, fader

inserts.title: Plugins
inserts.what: Per strip and per output, in the order you set

engine.title: Its own real-time engine
engine.text: Gain, fader, pan and summing, the EQ bank, gate and compressor, delay, reverb and an analyser tap run in one native C node inside PipeWire, not a pile of loopback processes.

stagebox.title: Stagebox in, PA out
stagebox.text: 40 channels at 96 kHz over native REAC. Roland S-4000S, S-1608 and S-4000H stageboxes join sample-synchronous.

surface.title: Every device is a surface
surface.text: One console, any number of browsers at once: a laptop at front of house, a tablet on stage, a phone on the floor. Touch, keyboard and mouse all work.

xtouch.title: Real faders under your hands
xtouch.text: Behringer X-Touch units drive the same fader map the console owns: motor faders, encoders, scribble strips and meters, each unit its own client.

features.f1: Aux and group buses, sends with pre and post taps
features.f4: Stereo linking and per-channel head gain
features.f6: Peak-hold meters and EBU R128 loudness on the mains
features.f7: The real latency of every step and plugin, live
features.f9: Adapters for Midas, X32/M32 and Roland consoles

stands.lead: The native engine mixes real shows.
stands.rig: It runs on a real rig, a Roland stagebox and an RME Babyface Pro. Phantom power was confirmed at the XLR pins, two stageboxes have run at once, and the rate has been switched between 48 and 96 kHz with the house up.
stands.missing: Some parts are not there yet. Of the control surfaces, only the X-Touch has been tested on real hardware. The plugin hosts are packaged today; the console itself is not published yet.
stands.features: {link} marks each item by how far it has been proven and lists the known limitations.

finished.eyebrow: How anything here gets called finished
finished.quote: If a control claims to affect audio, measure audio.
finished.text: A control can read back perfectly and reach nothing at all. So the processing is checked against values worked out on paper, changes are checked on the running audio graph, and a phantom power claim needs a person at the connector, never a light on a screen.

native.title: The processing a show lives on, written for the console itself.
native.lede: OpenMixer's own processors run inside the real-time mix node: no plugin host, no process boundary, no added latency. Every stage keeps the same promises. It never outputs a broken sample, it never stalls the audio thread, and when bypassed its output is exactly its input. {link} shows how to use each one.

eq.name: Interactive EQ
eq.what: Parametric bands drawn over the channel's live curve, dragged by hand.

gate.name: Gate
gate.what: With keyed detection from any source.

comp.name: Compressor
comp.what: Threshold, ratio, knee, attack, release and make-up, with its transfer curve.

expander.name: Expander · limiter · ducker
expander.what: Each a type either dynamics stage can take.

drive.name: Drive
drive.what: A saturator with four curves (soft, tape, tube and exciter), a character control from hard odd harmonics to warm even ones, full, low, high or tilt bands, and auto gain so it changes colour, not loudness.

chorus.name: Chorus · flanger
chorus.what: Modulation effects on the same Native FX chip.

fbs.name: FBS, feedback suppression
fbs.what: Hears a ring and cuts a narrow notch at its frequency, per channel, off until you arm it. Ring-out mode, for soundcheck, keeps its notches: they are a fact about the room. Live mode, for the show, lifts each cut back to 0 dB once the frequency stays clean.

hrp.name: HRP, harmonic resonance processor
hrp.what: Follows the note being played, finds the harmonic that is louder than it should be on that instrument, and cuts it as it moves. Monitor shows the cut it would make; Adaptive makes safe cuts by itself.

align.name: Align
align.what: Two microphones on one source, such as kick in and out or snare top and bottom, made to arrive together.

rta.name: RTA
rta.what: A real-time analyser tapped straight from the engine.

plugins.title: Every plugin you want. Never at the cost of the show.
plugins.lede: A live console cannot go silent because a plugin crashed. So OpenMixer loads processing in layers: its own code inside the engine, and outside plugins in supervised processes that can fail without touching anything else. {link}.

native.title: OpenMixer native
native.text: Everything above, from the EQ and the whole dynamics family to FBS, HRP and Align, runs in the same real-time node as the mix, so it never crosses a process boundary.

open.title: LV2 and CLAP
open.text: The engine racks LV2 and CLAP plugins through one CLAP host: the adapter libomx-clap-lv2 presents each LV2 plugin as a CLAP plugin, so the console drives both formats the same way. Each plugin's controls come from its own metadata, and a catalog ranks plugins by measured latency so the live-safe choice comes first.

hostd.title: plugin-hostd
hostd.text: A supervisor between the console and its plugin hosts, each host running as a worker process: omx-clap-host for CLAP and for LV2 through its adapter, and mod-host for an LV2 plugin the adapter refuses. When a plugin crashes, plugin-hostd restarts only that worker and restores its plugins and every setting. That strip passes dry audio meanwhile, and every other channel carries on.

crash.title: A plugin dies mid-show. The mix does not notice.
crash.intro: We crash a plugin on purpose, on a running console, and measure every strip through it. This is what the console hears, in order:

timeline.worker_died: The worker holding the faulty plugin exits. Its strip passes dry.
timeline.worker_backoff: plugin-hostd waits, so a plugin that keeps crashing cannot flood the machine.
timeline.instance_restored: The plugin is loaded again, with every parameter as you left it.

crash.bitIdenticalText: The mix through plugin-hostd against the mix through today's host: not one sample differs.
crash.dbText: How far every other strip moved while one plugin crashed and came back.
crash.workerText: Only the worker holding the faulty plugin restarted, and only that plugin was loaded again.
crash.measured: Measured on the OpenMixer development console.

open.title: Built in the open, for everyone who hosts plugins.
open.lede: The pieces OpenMixer uses to load outside plugins are projects of their own, packaged for Fedora and Debian, including Raspberry Pi OS and Zynthian. Any host that already speaks mod-host's protocol can use them.

repos.clapHost: A CLAP and LV2 plugin host for JACK, driven over mod-host's socket protocol. It runs LV2 plugins natively through lilv, with the adapter libomx-clap-lv2 mapping them to CLAP ports. It hosts effects and instruments with MIDI in, runs on its own the way jalv does for LV2, and ships omx-clap-scan to list what a CLAP bundle holds.
repos.hostd: The plugin supervisor. It speaks mod-host's protocol to its clients and runs each plugin in a worker of a native host: omx-clap-host for CLAP, and for LV2 the adapter first, with mod-host only for a plugin the adapter refuses. It brings crash isolation, restart with back-off and state replay.
repos.protocol: mod-host's socket protocol as a shared library, so a second host can speak it without carrying a copy. Proposed to mod-host and packaged for Fedora; both hosts above link it.

install.lede: Every package is built from a release tag, signed, and published here, for Fedora, Debian, Raspberry Pi OS and Zynthian. Add the repository, install, and run.

upstream.title: What OpenMixer is built on.
upstream.text: None of these are ours. They are the projects the console would not exist without, and the ones to read if you want to understand the layer underneath it.
upstream.pipewire: The audio graph the console lives in. OpenMixer's engine is a native PipeWire client and its signal processing is a filter node in that graph.

reading.title: How a verdict is reached.
reading.one: A plugin is tested once for each way it can be offered. It is accepted when one of those ways passes every measurement, accepted with conditions when the best it can do is to run in a process of its own, and refused when it can be offered in no way.
reading.two: The long-run stability test was not part of these records, so no plugin was judged on it either way.
